Math.title: Math week: multiplication, division, and elapsed time
Math.subject: Math
Math.contentMarkdown:
![Array model shows six rows of six and a separate 36-counter model grouped by four](images/grade-03/math/g03-math-array-and-groups.png)

The model has two parts. In the array, count six rows with six counters in each row: 6 × 6 = 36. In the second part, split those 36 counters into groups of four: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 groups. The two operations describe the same total in different ways. Use the blank lines to record the number of rows, counters in each row, total, and groups.

![Elapsed-time number line counts from 6:00 a.m. to 6:30 a.m. in two 15-minute jumps](images/grade-03/math/g03-math-elapsed-time-number-line.png)

The shown interval is 30 minutes: 6:00 to 6:15, then 6:15 to 6:30. A number line makes the passage of time visible. For other questions, start at the given time and add jumps that are easy to track, such as 10, 15, or 30 minutes. Check the hour as well as the minutes.

**What is verified:** P.S. 230 names TERC Investigations as the basis of its math program, but does not publish the current Grade 3 lesson order. The New York State Grade 3 standards include multiplication and division, measurement, and telling time to the nearest minute. The authentic state-test examples below are NYSED 2025 Grade 3 Math Session 2, Questions 37 and 38 (printed pages 10–11). The extra lesson examples and drills are newly written practice; they are not school assignments or released test items. [P.S. 230 math page](http://www.ps230.org/mathematics); [New York State Grade 3 math standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/nys-next-generation-mathematics-p-12-standards.pdf); [NYSED 2025 Grade 3 math booklet](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf).

#### Learn the ideas

**Equal groups and multiplication.** Multiplication can count equal groups quickly. If there are 4 bags with 3 apples in each, the groups are 3 + 3 + 3 + 3. That is 4 groups of 3, or 4 × 3 = 12 apples. The first factor tells how many groups; the second tells how many are in each group. In an array, rows show groups and objects in each row show the group size. Count by rows or columns to check the total.

**Division as sharing or grouping.** Division can ask how many are in each equal share, or how many equal groups can be made. For 20 counters shared among 5 children, 20 ÷ 5 = 4 counters each. For 20 counters put into groups of 5, 20 ÷ 5 = 4 groups. The answer is 4 in both stories, but the unit label changes. Multiplication checks the result: 5 × 4 = 20.

**Related facts.** The same three numbers make a multiplication/division fact family. From 3 × 8 = 24, we can write 8 × 3 = 24, 24 ÷ 3 = 8, and 24 ÷ 8 = 3. The array can help show why these facts belong together. To solve an unknown factor such as 6 × ? = 42, ask how many groups of 6 make 42; 42 ÷ 6 = 7.

**Elapsed time.** Elapsed time is how much time passes from a start to an end. One useful way to find it is to count forward on a number line. For 2:35 to 3:05, jump 25 minutes to 3:00, then 5 more minutes to 3:05. The total is 30 minutes. For 9:50 plus 25 minutes, jump 10 minutes to 10:00, then 15 minutes to 10:15. When a problem asks for the start time, count backward from the end time. Always state whether the answer is a time of day or a length of time: “4:00” is a clock time; “40 minutes” is a duration.

**How to show clear work.** Draw groups or an array for multiplication. For division, write the total and the group size or number of shares, then label what the answer counts. For time, mark the start, each jump, and the end. Estimate first: adding 30 minutes should move the clock about half an hour. If the exact answer is far from that estimate, check the jumps.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60 minute plan |
|---|---|
| 1 — Build equal groups | Spend 10 minutes making groups with counters or drawings. Spend 15 minutes writing repeated addition and multiplication for each picture. Spend 15 minutes making arrays and counting rows and columns. Finish by explaining what each factor means in two story problems. |
| 2 — Divide and check | Model both sharing and making groups. Solve at least six problems with counters, sketches, or equations. For each answer, multiply back to check. Circle the unit word: groups, objects in each group, or shares for each person. |
| 3 — Connect the facts | Use arrays to make multiplication/division fact families. Fill missing factors and missing totals. Create one story for each equation, then trade stories with a partner and check whether the equation matches. |
| 4 — Find elapsed time | Practice forward and backward jumps on a blank number line. Begin with times within one hour, then cross an hour boundary. Label every jump and add the minutes. Explain the difference between the ending clock time and the number of minutes that passed. |
| 5 — State-item study and mixed review | Solve the two NYSED released items described below without looking at the answers. Then complete the supplemental set, correct errors in a different color, and write one sentence explaining a strategy that worked. |

#### Authentic released examples

In **NYSED 2025 Grade 3 Math Session 2, Question 38**, a baker places 6 cookies in each of 6 bags, then makes the same number of brownies and puts 4 brownies in each bag. First find the cookie total: 6 × 6 = 36 cookies. The brownie total is also 36, so 36 ÷ 4 = **9 brownie bags**. The first answer counts cookies; the second counts bags. The source item is on printed page 11.

In **Question 37**, Cassandra wakes at a quarter past 6 in the morning, and her bus comes one-half hour later. A quarter past 6 is 6:15 a.m. Add 30 minutes: 6:15 → 6:30 → **6:45 a.m.** The source item is on printed page 10. These summaries preserve the math task while avoiding copying the full test page. [NYSED released booklet](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf).

#### Supplemental practice — newly written, not school or state-test questions

Show a picture, equation, or number-line jumps. Add the unit to every answer.

1. There are 7 plates with 4 crackers on each plate. How many crackers are there?
2. Put 36 counters into groups of 6. How many groups can you make?
3. A room has 5 rows of 8 chairs. Write an equation and find the number of chairs.
4. Put 42 pencils into boxes with 7 pencils in each. How many boxes are needed?
5. Share 32 cards equally among 4 players. How many cards does each player get?
6. Find the missing factor: 6 × □ = 42. Check with a division equation.
7. A lesson starts at 2:35 and ends at 3:05. How long is it?
8. A show starts at 9:50 and lasts 25 minutes. When does it end?
9. A bus arrives at 8:05. It takes 45 minutes to get there. When did it leave?
10. A game begins at 4:10 and lasts 35 minutes. When does it end?
11. A class ends at 6:40, which is 20 minutes after it began. What was the start time?
12. Write the four related facts that use 3, 8, and 24.

Math.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer key

1. **28 crackers:** 7 × 4 = 28.
2. **6 groups:** 36 ÷ 6 = 6; check 6 × 6 = 36.
3. **40 chairs:** 5 × 8 = 40.
4. **6 boxes:** 42 ÷ 7 = 6; check 6 × 7 = 42.
5. **8 cards each:** 32 ÷ 4 = 8; check 4 × 8 = 32.
6. **7:** 42 ÷ 6 = 7, so 6 × 7 = 42.
7. **30 minutes:** 2:35 → 3:00 is 25 minutes, then 5 more minutes.
8. **10:15:** 9:50 → 10:00 is 10 minutes; 15 minutes remain.
9. **7:20:** count back 5 minutes to 8:00, then 40 more minutes.
10. **4:45:** 4:10 plus 30 minutes is 4:40; add 5.
11. **6:20:** count back 20 minutes from 6:40.
12. **3 × 8 = 24; 8 × 3 = 24; 24 ÷ 3 = 8; 24 ÷ 8 = 3.**

For each response, check the arithmetic, the unit, and whether the drawing or jumps match the story. If an answer is wrong, ask whether the mistake was the operation, the group size, the time jump, or the label.

Math.title: Math week: area, arrays, and perimeter
Math.subject: Math
Math.contentMarkdown:
**School and grade scope:** P.S. 230 confirms TERC Investigations as its mathematics program, but its public newsletters do not confirm this exact area-and-perimeter week or current pacing. This unit uses New York State Grade 3 standards and four actual questions from the Spring 2025 NYSED Grade 3 math release. They are grade-level practice, not a claim that Nahid's class is studying these exact tasks. [New York State math standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/nys-next-generation-mathematics-p-12-standards_0.pdf) · [2025 NYSED Grade 3 Mathematics released questions and answer map](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf).

#### Learn the ideas

**Area is how much flat space a shape covers.** A unit square is a square with side lengths of one unit. Its area is one square unit. If a shape is covered with unit squares without spaces or overlaps, count the squares to find the area. Write square units, such as square centimeters, because area covers a surface.

**A rectangle can be counted by rows.** If each row has the same number of unit squares, multiplication is faster than counting one square at a time. For a rectangle with 6 columns and 4 rows, there are `6+6+6+6` squares, or `6×4 = 24 square units`. The side lengths are 6 units and 4 units. Keep the number of rows and columns visible in a drawing so the multiplication has a clear meaning.

**A complicated shape can be split into rectangles.** Draw a cut that separates the shape into rectangles that do not overlap. Find each rectangle's area, then add. If a small rectangular part is missing from a larger rectangle, find the large area and subtract the missing area. Mark the pieces on the picture so no part is left out or counted twice.

**Perimeter is the distance around a shape.** It measures the outside boundary and uses regular length units, such as centimeters or meters. Add the outside side lengths. For a rectangle, opposite sides match, so `perimeter = length + width + length + width`. Do not use the area multiplication to find the perimeter. A 6-unit by 4-unit rectangle has area `24 square units` and perimeter `20 units`—two different measurements with different units.

**The same area can have different perimeters.** A 3-by-7 rectangle and a 4-by-6 rectangle both have perimeter 20 units, but their areas are 21 and 24 square units. The measurements answer different questions: area asks how many unit squares cover the inside; perimeter asks how far it is around the outside.

#### Five-session study plan — about 55–65 minutes each

| Session | Lesson and source work | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Cover and count | Read the area explanation. Draw a rectangle with 4 rows and 6 columns of unit squares. Count by rows, then multiply. Open NYSED 2025 question 12 in the source PDF and solve from its actual diagram. | A 4-by-6 grid with `24 square units`, plus the source question's answer and a note showing how its squares were counted. |
| 2 — Use arrays to find area | Make three rectangles with square tiles or grid paper. Write repeated addition and a multiplication equation for each. Then solve released NYSED question 30: the rectangle has area 15 square units; decide how many unit squares cover it. | Three labeled arrays and the source answer with its square-unit reasoning. |
| 3 — Split and combine | Draw an L-shaped figure on grid paper. Split it into two non-overlapping rectangles. Find both areas and add. Compare that with putting the L-shape inside one larger rectangle and subtracting its missing corner. Open released question 20 and solve from the original partial-cover model. | Two different correct methods for the same L-shape and the official answer to question 20 supported by the source figure. |
| 4 — Separate area from perimeter | For a rectangle, trace the outside edge in one color and the inside unit squares in another. Write the correct units beside each result. Solve released question 28 using the playground's dimensions in the source figure; read the item map for the official key. | One area/perimeter comparison and the source playground calculation with square meters. |
| 5 — Explain and check | Complete the 12 transfer drills. Choose two answers and explain why one uses square units and the other uses length units. Revisit any wrong item by drawing or marking the shape; do not memorize a letter without its reason. | Corrected drill sheet and a short explanation that separates area from perimeter. |

#### Authentic NYSED practice — use the original figures

The complete questions and diagrams are in the linked NYSED PDF. The guide does not copy their figures. Each answer below is checked against NYSED's official answer map; students should still show how the figure supports the keyed response.

- **Question 12, Session 1:** a rectangle is made of unit squares; find its area. The official map keys **D (21)** and maps the item to NY-3.MD.7a. Count its actual squares or count equal rows; do not infer the answer from the letter alone.
- **Question 20, Session 1:** a model is partly covered with unit squares; find the area when the model is fully covered. The official map keys **C (27 square units)** and maps the item to NY-3.MD.6. Use the original diagram to see the complete outline.
- **Question 28, Session 2:** use the playground side lengths shown in the booklet to find area. The official map keys **C (45 square meters)** and maps it to NY-3.MD.7d. Use the source figure; do not guess its dimensions from the answer choices.
- **Question 30, Session 2:** a rectangle has area 15 square units; how many unit squares cover it without gaps or overlaps? The official map keys **C (15)** and maps the item to NY-3.MD.5b.

These released examples show the kinds of models and reasoning assessed. NYSED notes that released questions are not the full range of what should be taught; this week also practices side lengths, composite shapes, and explaining why the units differ.

#### Extra practice — written for this guide, not copied from a test or school lesson

1. A rectangle has 5 rows of 4 unit squares. Find the area.
2. A rectangle is 8 units long and 3 units wide. Find the area using multiplication.
3. A rectangle has area 54 square centimeters and width 6 centimeters. How many rows of 1-square-centimeter tiles cover it?
4. A shape is made from a 4-by-3 rectangle and a 2-by-3 rectangle joined along one edge without overlap. Find its area.
5. A 6-by-5 rectangle has a 2-by-2 corner removed. Find the remaining area.
6. Find the area and perimeter of a rectangle 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. Include units.
7. A rectangle has side lengths 9 m and 2 m. Find its area and perimeter.
8. Which has the greater area: a 3-by-7 rectangle or a 4-by-6 rectangle? Compare their perimeters too.
9. A rectangular garden has area 32 square meters and width 4 meters. Find its length.
10. A student says the perimeter of a 5-by-3 rectangle is `5×3 = 15 cm`. Explain the mistake and give the correct perimeter.
11. A path goes around a 7 m by 5 m garden. How many meters of edging are needed to go around once? How many square meters of soil cover the garden?
12. Draw two different rectangles with area 24 square units. Find both perimeters. What does this show?

**Checked answer key:** 1) `5×4 = 20 square units`. 2) `8×3 = 24 square units`. 3) `54÷6 = 9 rows`. 4) `4×3 + 2×3 = 12+6 = 18 square units`. 5) `6×5−2×2 = 30−4 = 26 square units`. 6) Area `6×4 = 24 cm²`; perimeter `6+4+6+4 = 20 cm`. 7) Area `9×2 = 18 m²`; perimeter `9+2+9+2 = 22 m`. 8) The 3-by-7 area is 21; the 4-by-6 area is 24, so 4-by-6 is larger. Both perimeters are 20 units. 9) `32÷4 = 8 m`. 10) Multiplication finds area, not distance around. Perimeter is `5+3+5+3 = 16 cm`. 11) Edging: `7+5+7+5 = 24 m`; soil: `7×5 = 35 m²`. 12) Many answers work. For example, 4-by-6 has perimeter 20; 3-by-8 has perimeter 22. Both have area 24 square units, so equal area does not require equal perimeter.

#### Visual plan

Use the original diagrams beside NYSED questions 12, 20, and 28 in the linked PDF. The code-drawn study visual below is a guide aid, not a reproduction of the test artwork.

![Unit-square grids show a 4-by-6 rectangle, its outside perimeter, a missing-corner area, and two rectangles with equal perimeters](images/grade-03/math/g03-math-area-and-perimeter.png)

This guide's four exact question contexts come from the public NYSED 2025 release, and its 12 extra drills are written for this guide. Neither set should be labeled as Nahid's current homework or textbook page without a school assignment confirming it.

Math.title: Math week: fractions as equal parts and points on a number line
Math.subject: Math
Math.contentMarkdown:
**School and grade scope:** P.S. 230 confirms TERC Investigations as its math program, but its public sources do not confirm that Nahid's class is on this unit now. Fractions are part of the New York Grade 3 standards. This week focuses on making equal parts, reading a fraction, locating fractions from 0 to 1, and comparing simple fractions with pictures or number lines. It follows NY-3.NF.1–3 and uses one actual released NYSED example. [New York State Grade 3 math standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/nys-next-generation-mathematics-p-12-standards_0.pdf) · [2025 NYSED Grade 3 Math released questions](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf) · [2025 NYSED Grade 3 Math scoring materials](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-scoring-materials-math-g3.pdf).

#### Learn it in plain English

**A fraction names equal parts of one whole.** First decide what counts as the whole: one sandwich, one strip, one group, or the space from 0 to 1 on a number line. Then split that whole into equal-sized parts. If the parts are not equal, they are not fourths or thirds just because someone drew three or four pieces.

In `3/4`, the bottom number, 4, tells how many equal parts make one whole. The top number, 3, tells how many of those parts we are counting. So `3/4` means three of four equal parts. The fraction bar means the whole is being divided into equal parts; it does not mean the pieces can have different sizes.

**A unit fraction names one equal part.** If one whole is split into 5 equal parts, one part is `1/5`. Five copies of `1/5` make the whole: `5/5 = 1`. In general, one copy of `1/b` is one of `b` equal parts, and `b/b` is one whole when those parts all belong to the same whole.

**Fractions are numbers, so they can sit on a number line.** Between 0 and 1, split the distance into the number of equal jumps named by the denominator. For fourths, make four equal jumps. The first mark is `1/4`, the next is `2/4`, then `3/4`, and the last mark is `4/4 = 1`. Keep the whole interval the same size when comparing lines.

**Compare only after checking the whole and the parts.** If two fractions have the same denominator, their parts have the same size; the fraction with more parts is greater. So `5/8 > 3/8`. If two fractions have the same numerator and the same whole, compare the size of each part: thirds are larger than fourths, so `2/3 > 2/4`. Draw a model or number line to check. Do not use a shortcut before checking that the parts are equal and refer to the same-sized whole.

At this level, build fractions with equal parts, number lines, and drawings. Do not change unlike denominators to compare them by a rule the student has not learned; use models to reason. These lessons do not teach decimal notation or fraction multiplication.

#### Authentic released example

NYSED's Spring 2025 Grade 3 Math Question 36 gives a whole pie split into equal pieces, says one piece is `1/8` of the whole, and asks how many pieces there are and why. The answer is **8 pieces**: the denominator tells how many equal pieces make the whole. The official scoring material explains that a complete response must identify the number of pieces and show the fraction reasoning; writing only `1/8` does not answer how many pieces. Use the original item and scoring examples from the linked NYSED PDFs, printed test page 10; this summary does not copy the test figure. [Released item, Question 36](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf) · [Official scoring materials](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-scoring-materials-math-g3.pdf).

#### Five-session study plan — 50–60 minutes each

| Session | Lesson and practice | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Make equal parts | Use paper strips or the first image panel. Fold or draw one strip into 2 equal parts, another into 3, and another into 4. Shade one part in each. Say the denominator first, then the numerator. Make one uneven drawing and explain why its pieces cannot be named thirds. | Three equal-part models labeled `1/2`, `1/3`, and `1/4`, plus one corrected non-example. |
| 2 — Put fractions on a line | Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Split it into 4 equal intervals and mark `0/4`, `1/4`, `2/4`, `3/4`, `4/4`. Then draw a second line in thirds and keep the whole interval the same length. | Two number lines with equal spacing, correct labels, and `4/4 = 1`. |
| 3 — Compare fractions with same denominators | Use same-length strips split into eighths. Shade `3/8` and `5/8`; compare the number of equal parts. Repeat with `1/4` and `3/4`. Explain why the bottom numbers match. | Two written comparisons and a sentence: “The parts are the same size because…” |
| 4 — Compare same numerators and compose a whole | Make bars split into thirds and fourths. Shade `2/3` and `2/4`; compare the actual shaded lengths. Build a whole from copies of `1/6` and name it `6/6`. | A model-supported comparison and a unit-fraction chain ending at one whole. |
| 5 — Solve the real released item and explain | Work through NYSED Question 36 from the original booklet. Draw your own eight-part circle or strip model after answering; do not copy the test diagram. Then complete the new practice and correct any response that confuses the number of pieces with the number shaded. | The official item response with a labeled model and a complete sentence explaining why there are eight equal pieces. |

#### New practice — written for this guide, not copied from NYSED or TERC

1. A strip is split into 5 equal parts. One part is shaded. What fraction is shaded?
2. A rectangle is split into 4 equal parts. Three parts are shaded. Write the fraction and say what each number tells you.
3. One of 6 equal slices of the same-size pizza is one what fraction of the whole?
4. A student draws three pieces, but one piece is twice as wide as the other two. Can the student call all three pieces thirds? Explain.
5. On a number line from 0 to 1 split into 4 equal jumps, what fraction is at the third mark after 0?
6. A number line from 0 to 1 has 8 equal jumps. What fraction is at the fifth mark after 0?
7. How many one-fourth pieces make one whole? Write a fraction equation.
8. Which is greater: `5/8` or `3/8`? Explain using equal parts.
9. Which is greater: `2/3` or `2/4`? Use a drawing or explain how the part sizes compare.
10. Put these in order from least to greatest: `3/4`, `1/4`, `2/4`.
11. A sandwich is cut into 6 equal pieces. A student eats 1 piece. What fraction is left?
12. In NYSED 2025 Question 36, each equal pie piece is `1/8` of the whole. How many pieces make the whole? Explain what the denominator tells you.
13. Three same-sized pieces each equal `1/4` of one whole. What fraction of the whole do the three pieces cover?
14. In `2/5`, name the numerator and denominator. What does each tell you?
15. Draw a bar split into 5 equal parts and shade `2/5`. Label the whole and the parts.
16. Which is greater: `3/4` or `3/6`? Compare the size of one part before deciding.
17. A student writes `4/4 = 4` because the top number is 4. Explain the error and give the correct value.
18. Show with two same-length bars why `2/4` and `1/2` name the same amount.

#### Checked answer key

1. `1/5`.
2. `3/4`; the 4 means the whole has four equal parts, and the 3 means three are shaded.
3. `1/6`.
4. No. Thirds must be three equal-sized parts of the same whole.
5. `3/4`.
6. `5/8`.
7. Four; `1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1`.
8. `5/8`; both fractions have eighths, and five equal eighth-parts are more than three.
9. `2/3`; with the same whole and same number of parts counted, each third is larger than each fourth.
10. `1/4 < 2/4 < 3/4`.
11. `5/6`.
12. Eight pieces; the denominator 8 names eight equal pieces in one whole.
13. `3/4`.
14. Numerator 2: the number of parts counted; denominator 5: the number of equal parts in the whole.
15. Check for five equal parts, exactly two shaded, and a label `2/5`.
16. `3/4`; both fractions count three parts, but fourths are larger than sixths when they describe the same-sized whole.
17. The 4 counts equal parts in the whole; it does not mean four wholes. `4/4 = 1` whole.
18. Both bars must be the same length; shading two of four equal pieces covers half, the same length as one of two equal pieces.

Math.title: Math week: place value, addition, and subtraction within 1,000
Math.subject: Math
Math.contentMarkdown:
**School and grade scope:** P.S. 230 confirms TERC Investigations as its mathematics program; it does not publish Nahid's current lesson calendar. This is a grade-level support week aligned to New York's Grade 3 standards for rounding, adding and subtracting within 1,000, and understanding four-digit place value. The official standards say students should use place-value ideas, operation properties, and the link between addition and subtraction. This guide adds practice; it does not identify a TERC lesson or claim the teacher assigned this topic now. [NYSED Grade 3 math standards snapshot](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/nys-math-standards-grade-3-snapshot.pdf) · [2025 NYSED Grade 3 Math released questions and answer map](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf).

#### Read and learn the ideas

**A digit's place tells its value.** In `3,958`, the 3 means 3 thousands, the 9 means 9 hundreds, the 5 means 5 tens, and the 8 means 8 ones. We can write the same number in expanded form: `3,000 + 900 + 50 + 8`. The digit 5 is not just “5”; in the tens place it is worth 50.

Read the same number as **three thousand, nine hundred fifty-eight**. The comma separates the thousands group from the hundreds, tens, and ones. A zero in a place keeps the other digits in the right positions: `6,042` is six thousand forty-two, with 0 hundreds and 4 tens.

**Ten of one place make one of the next place.** Ten ones can be regrouped as one ten. Ten tens can be regrouped as one hundred. Ten hundreds can be regrouped as one thousand. The total value does not change when pieces are traded: `14 ones = 1 ten + 4 ones`. This is why adding 8 ones and 6 ones gives 14 ones, which can be written as 1 ten and 4 ones.

**Add by place, then regroup.** For `278 + 156`, add the ones: `8 + 6 = 14`, or 1 ten and 4 ones. Add the tens: `7 + 5 + 1 carried ten = 13 tens`, or 1 hundred and 3 tens. Add the hundreds: `2 + 1 + 1 carried hundred = 4 hundreds`. The answer is `434`. Expanded form shows the same idea: `200 + 70 + 8 + 100 + 50 + 6 = 300 + 120 + 14 = 434`.

**Subtract by keeping the value while regrouping.** In `503 − 278`, there are 5 hundreds, 0 tens, and 3 ones. There are not enough ones to take away 8 ones, so exchange 1 hundred for 10 tens, then 1 ten for 10 ones. Now the same 503 is 4 hundreds, 9 tens, and 13 ones. Subtract: `13 − 8 = 5` ones, `9 − 7 = 2` tens, and `4 − 2 = 2` hundreds. The answer is `225`. Check with addition: `225 + 278 = 503`.

**Use a number line or expanded form when it helps.** For `640 − 285`, subtract 200, then 80, then 5: `640 → 440 → 360 → 355`. The inverse check is `355 + 285 = 640`. A written algorithm is a useful record only if each regrouped digit still represents the same total value.

**Round to estimate, then keep the exact answer.** To round 347 to the nearest ten, compare it to 340 and 350; it is closer to 350. To round 347 to the nearest hundred, compare it to 300 and 400; it is closer to 300. To estimate `398 + 207`, round to the nearest hundred: `398` is about `400`, and `207` is about `200`, so the sum should be about `600`. The exact sum is `605`, which is close to the estimate. Rounding helps catch a misplaced digit, but it does not replace the exact answer when a problem asks for one.

#### Exact released example: read the place value

The 2025 NYSED Grade 3 Mathematics release includes Question 17: students identify the tens-place digit in `3,958`. The correct option is **B, 5**; that digit's value is **50**. The official answer map keys B and associates the item with four-digit place value. This is a real state-test item, not proof that P.S. 230 assigned it. [NYSED released booklet and official item map](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf), Question 17, printed page 8.

#### Five-session study plan — 50–60 minutes each

| Session | Lesson and practice | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Name the place and value | Read the first two explanations. Use a place-value chart for `3,958`; say the value of each digit, read the number name, and write the expanded form. Then answer released Question 17 from the original booklet. | A labeled chart, number name, expanded form, and a sentence explaining why the tens digit 5 has value 50. |
| 2 — Add with regrouping | Build `276 + 158` with drawings, base-ten blocks, or the base-ten place-value visual. Trade 10 ones for 1 ten and 10 tens for 1 hundred. Then solve it in expanded form and with a written algorithm; compare the records. | Both methods showing the same total, `434`, and a note naming each trade. |
| 3 — Subtract across a zero | Model `503 − 278`. Show both exchanges so the ones and tens can be subtracted. Check the result with addition. Also solve `600 − 347` using a number line or regrouping. | A before/after place-value drawing and inverse checks for both answers. |
| 4 — Estimate and solve word problems | Round each three-digit number to the nearest hundred to estimate. Then solve exact problems. In the word problems, underline the question and label the quantities before choosing an operation. | One estimate beside each exact answer, with units or object labels from the story. |
| 5 — Mix the skills and explain | Complete the 18 guide questions below without a calculator. Circle any regrouping step and check every subtraction with addition. Rework any answer that differs greatly from its estimate. | Corrected practice with one written explanation of an addition and one of a subtraction. |

#### New practice — written for this guide, not copied from NYSED or TERC

2. In `3,958`, what is the tens digit, and what is its value?
3. Write `3,958` in expanded form.

13. A student says `503 − 278 = 375` because 8 ones cannot be taken from 3 ones, so the student writes 3 on top. What place-value step is missing?

15. Add `340 + 250` by place value. Write the expanded-form steps.
16. Subtract `921 − 487`. Check using addition.
17. A classroom has 368 storybooks and receives 257 more. How many storybooks are there now? Write an equation and a sentence.
18. A paper supply starts with 720 sheets. The class uses 286 sheets. How many sheets remain? Write an equation and check it.
19. Round 347 to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred. Explain which two nearby numbers you compared each time.
20. Use the number from released Question 17, `3,958`, to estimate the nearest ten and nearest hundred. This is a guide-created rounding prompt, not part of the released question.

Math.title: Math week: mass, liquid volume, and scaled graphs
Math.subject: Math
Math.contentMarkdown:
**School and grade scope:** P.S. 230 confirms TERC Investigations as its math program, but the current class sequence is not public. This week supports NY-3.MD.2a–b and NY-3.MD.3: estimate and measure mass or liquid volume, solve one-step problems using the same units, and read or build scaled graphs. The standard uses grams, kilograms, and liters; it excludes geometric volume and says not to combine different units in these word problems. It does not confirm that this is Nahid's current TERC unit. [NYSED Grade 3 math standards crosswalk](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/nys-math-standards-grade-3-crosswalk.pdf) · [2025 NYSED Grade 3 released math test](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf).

#### Learn it in plain English

**Mass and liquid volume measure different things.** Mass tells how much matter an object has; use grams (g) or kilograms (kg). Liquid volume tells how much liquid is in a container; use liters (L). A balance or scale helps measure mass. A container with marked lines helps measure liquid volume. Read the unit printed on the tool before recording a number. Estimate first, then measure and compare the estimate with the result.

**Use the same unit throughout a calculation.** If a problem says 12 liters are shared equally among 6 containers, divide `12 ÷ 6 = 2`; each container gets 2 liters. Keep the unit: `2 L`. This standard's word problems give the amounts in the same unit. Do not add grams to kilograms or liters to grams. These lessons do not ask students to convert units or find the space inside a solid box.

**A graph is a picture of data.** A title tells what the data describe. The category labels tell what is being compared. The scale tells how much each step on an axis means. A bar's height must line up with a scale mark. A bar graph may count by 2s, 5s, or 10s, so one small step may stand for more than one item. Read the scale before comparing bars; do not count each line as one unless the graph says so.

**A source can show more than one kind of measurement.** The National Weather Service posts a Central Park temperature-and-precipitation chart based on 30-year climate normals. The accompanying table says its averages use 1991–2020 data and was updated January 1, 2026. A normal is a long-term average; it is not the temperature or rainfall on one particular day, and it is not a forecast. The chart has separate scales for temperature and precipitation. Compare temperature values with the temperature scale and precipitation values with the precipitation scale; the height of a temperature bar cannot be compared directly with a precipitation bar.

**Use real source data, and label any rounding.** The NWS table gives the monthly average maximum temperature for Central Park. To make a Grade 3 bar graph with a clear scale, this guide rounds each source value to the nearest ten degrees Fahrenheit. The rounded graph is an approximate view; keep the original source values beside it so rounding does not hide the difference between months.

| Month | NWS average maximum (°F) | Rounded to nearest 10°F for student graph |
|---|---:|---:|
| January | 39.5 | 40 |
| February | 42.2 | 40 |
| March | 49.9 | 50 |
| April | 61.8 | 60 |
| May | 71.4 | 70 |
| June | 79.7 | 80 |
| July | 84.9 | 80 |
| August | 83.3 | 80 |
| September | 76.2 | 80 |
| October | 64.5 | 60 |
| November | 54.0 | 50 |
| December | 44.3 | 40 |

Source: National Weather Service, [Central Park, NY Normals and Extremes](https://www.weather.gov/media/okx/Climate/CentralPark/nycnormals.pdf), temperature records table. The table describes average daily maximum temperature for each month, not the highest temperature ever recorded in that month.

#### Authentic released example: divide liquid volume

NYSED's 2025 Grade 3 Mathematics Question 24 describes 12 liters of lemonade split equally among 6 containers. The correct choice is **A: 2 liters per container**. Show the division and write the unit: `12 L ÷ 6 = 2 L`. The official answer map keys A and maps this task to measurement/data and equal-group division. This is an actual released question, not evidence that P.S. 230 assigned it. [NYSED released booklet and answer map](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf), Question 24, printed page 11.

#### Five-session study plan — 50–60 minutes each

| Session | Lesson and practice | Evidence to keep |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Choose a unit and measure | Sort picture or classroom objects by whether mass or liquid volume would be measured. Estimate the mass of two safe objects, then use a scale that shows g or kg. If a liter-marked jug is available, estimate and measure a small amount of water with adult guidance; dry spills right away. Record the tool, unit, estimate, and measured amount. | A table of actual estimates and measurements. Do not fill it with made-up observations if no tool is available; use the released item instead. |
| 2 — Solve same-unit problems | Read the measurement explanation. Work through NYSED Question 24 from the original booklet. Model 12 L with a drawing split into 6 equal groups, then connect each group to `12 ÷ 6`. Solve the new measurement questions below and keep the unit in every answer. | A labeled six-group drawing, the released answer with units, and checked one-step calculations. |
| 3 — Read a real data source | Open the NWS chart and the normals table. Read the title, place, time period, units, and both scales. Find January and July in the table. Explain why a 30-year normal cannot tell you what today's temperature will be. | Source notes naming the data period, place, units, and one limit of the averages. |
| 4 — Build a scaled graph | Use the rounded-temperature column above. Draw a bar graph with months along the bottom and temperature on the side. Start at zero; make each equal step 10°F; label 0 through 80°F; draw 12 bars at the correct heights; include a title and note that the data are rounded normals. | A graph with equal bars/steps, complete labels, and a citation to the NWS table. |
| 5 — Read, compare, and explain | Answer the source questions and graph questions below. For any “how many more/less” response, name the two categories, read both scale values, and subtract. Mark the result as approximate when it comes from rounded data. | A corrected graph-reading sheet and one sentence explaining how rounding changed what can be compared. |

#### Source-based questions and new practice

Questions 1–4 refer to NYSED's released item, NYSED standards, and the NWS normals table. Questions 5–9 are hypothetical measurement practice, not measurements from P.S. 230 or a student. Questions 10–19 use NWS source values; their question wording is new practice for this guide. Question 20 uses a real tally collected by the class or tutor.

1. In NYSED Question 24, 12 liters are split equally among 6 containers. How many liters go in each container?
2. What two units are used to describe mass in the Grade 3 standard?
3. Which unit in the standard is used for liquid volume?
4. What years are the Central Park climate normals based on? Are they a forecast for today?
5. A balance shows an object has a mass of 275 g. A second object has a mass of 125 g. What is their combined mass?
6. A bag has 900 g of rice. A cook uses 275 g. How much rice remains?
7. Six equal bags contain a total of 750 g of seeds. How many grams are in each bag?
8. A jug contains 8 L of water. Another 3 L is poured in. How much is there now?
9. A 15 L container is shared equally among 3 pitchers. How many liters go into each pitcher?
10. In the NWS table, which month has the greatest average maximum temperature? Use the original table values, not only the rounded graph.
11. Round January's 39.5°F normal to the nearest ten degrees.
12. On the student graph, one step equals 10°F. How many steps high is a bar at 70°F?
13. Which months have rounded graph values of 40°F?
14. How many months have rounded graph values of 80°F?
15. About how many degrees higher is the rounded July value than the rounded January value?
16. The graph shows four months at 80°F after rounding. Does that prove their original average maximum temperatures were equal? Explain.
17. How many months are shown at either 40°F or 80°F in the rounded graph? Show the two counts and add.
18. A student says the 80°F July bar is shorter than the 4.60 inches of July precipitation because 80 is less than 4.60. What is wrong with this comparison?
19. The graph's title is “Central Park monthly normals.” What does the title tell you, and name one thing the graph does not tell you.
20. Draw a picture graph for 12 classroom objects sorted into 3 categories, using one picture for every 2 objects. Collect real counts first. What scale fact must be written in the key?

2. Grams and kilograms.
3. Liters.
4. 1991–2020; no, they are long-term averages, not a forecast for a particular day.
5. `275 g + 125 g = 400 g`.
6. `900 g − 275 g = 625 g`.
7. `750 g ÷ 6 = 125 g` per bag.
8. `8 L + 3 L = 11 L`.

10. July, at 84.9°F.
11. `40°F`.
12. 7 equal steps above zero.
13. January, February, and December.

17. `3 + 4 = 7` months.
18. The units and measurements are different. Temperature uses °F and precipitation uses inches, with separate graph scales. A larger or shorter bar on one scale cannot be compared directly with a bar on the other.
19. It shows long-term monthly climate averages for Central Park. It does not give today's conditions or predict tomorrow's weather.
20. Answers depend on the real tally. The graph key must say that one picture stands for 2 objects; the student must draw half as many pictures as the count for each category and label each bar/category. If a category count is odd, the student should use a half-picture or choose a different scale and explain it.

**Visual source:** Use the [National Weather Service Central Park temperature-and-precipitation chart](https://www.weather.gov/images/okx/Climate/CentralPark_TempPrecip_Normals.png) beside the NWS table. It is an authentic climate graphic, not a generated teaching image. Keep the two axis units separate. Students draw their own 10°F scaled bar graph from the linked temperature data; no additional AI image is needed for this week.

![Blank organizer for a nonfiction central idea, three pieces of evidence, paragraph locations, and explanation](images/grade-03/ela/g03-ela-nonfiction-evidence-organizer.png)

Fill the organizer from the actual passage. Put a paragraph number beside every fact and keep a fact separate from an inference.

**Source and school-scope note:** the Spring 2025 NYSED Grade 3 ELA booklet includes Meryl Magby's nonfiction passage *Raccoons*, first published in 2013. It appears on printed test pages 19–21; questions 19–25 are on printed pages 22–24. This is a genuine released assessment reading, not proof that P.S. 230 assigned this book or teaches it this year. The complete passage, graphic, questions, and official scoring materials are linked here: [NYSED released booklet](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/ela/2025/2025-released-items-ela-g3.pdf); [NYSED Grade 3 scoring materials](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/ela/2025/2025-scoring-materials-ela-g3.pdf).

#### Read it in simple English

Read the complete passage before using this short map. It begins with body facts and a graphic, then explains that raccoons eat plants and animals and that their food changes with where they live. It describes night feeding and marks one explanation as what scientists think, not a sure fact. Later sections cover daytime hiding, dens, winter behavior, and raccoons near people. Check the original for every paragraph number, example, and answer; this summary is not a replacement for the passage.

#### Five-session study plan (45–60 minutes per session)

| Session | Work | Save this evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Read for the whole idea | Read the entire passage once without answering the questions. Write a short note beside each section heading. On a second read, place a star beside details repeated or explained in more than one section. Tell the main idea in one sentence without listing every fact. | Heading notes and one first-draft central idea. |
| 2 — Match text and graphic | Reread the body-description section and inspect the original graphic in the NYSED booklet. Write three things a reader can see in the graphic and two facts that come from the words instead. Then explain which question the graphic helps answer. | A two-column “graphic shows / text tells” chart with the booklet page. |
| 3 — Follow headings and evidence | Answer official questions 19–23. For each, underline the clue in the passage, record the paragraph or section heading, and explain in one sentence why the clue fits. For one item, explain why a tempting answer is less supported. | Five answer notes tied to section or paragraph numbers. |
| 4 — Explain words and central idea | Answer official questions 24–25. For question 24, infer the meaning of “pests” from how the passage uses it and select two details that support the inference. For question 25, state a central idea and choose two details from different parts of the passage. | Two short answers; use complete sentences and paragraph clues. |
| 5 — Revise and teach back | Review the official scoring guide. Improve one weak answer by adding a missing detail or clearer explanation. Make a one-page study sheet with three headings, four paraphrased facts, one graphic observation, a central idea, and a source line. Do not copy the test passage or its graphic into a public website. | Final study sheet plus a two-sentence explanation of how evidence supports the main idea. |

#### Exact released-question answers

- **19: A.** The graphic helps by showing what raccoons look like.
- **20: C.** The passage says raccoons hide during the day to stay safe; this best explains why they mostly come out at night.
- **21: D.** “Many Different Dens” contains the winter information.
- **22: B.** The passage directly connects food choice with where a raccoon lives.
- **23: A.** The description “smart and quick” reveals the author's positive view.
- **24: Constructed response.** “Pests” means animals that cause trouble or unwanted problems for people. Two supporting details can be that raccoons tip over trash cans, dig through gardens, pull down bird feeders, or hide/have babies in unwanted places. Full-credit responses give a clear meaning and at least two relevant details; see the official scoring guide.
- **25: Constructed response.** A valid central idea summarizes what the passage teaches about raccoons. The scoring guide accepts different central ideas when two accurate details support them. One possible idea is that raccoons have body features and habits that help them find food and live in different places. Credit depends on the two matching details and explanation, not on using this exact sentence.

#### New practice (supplemental, not NYSED questions)

1. The passage says raccoon food depends on where the animal lives. Is that a fact or an inference? Give the paragraph clue.
2. A learner writes, “Raccoons dip food because they want to wash it.” What should the learner change to match the passage's level of certainty?
3. Name one detail the graphic can show quickly and one detail a reader must get from the words.
4. Which heading should a reader check for winter behavior? Explain how the heading helps.
5. In your own words, what does “nocturnal” mean?
6. Why is “raccoons are always dangerous” not supported by this passage?
7. Write one fact about dens and one inference a reader might make from it. Label both.
8. Choose two details that could support the idea that raccoons can find food near people.
9. Write a central idea in one sentence. Add two paragraph clues that support it.
10. How does the author show that raccoons can cause problems for people? Use two details.
11. What extra source would help check the claim that raccoon numbers may be growing?
12. Summarize the passage in two sentences without copying a sentence from the book.

#### Checked answer guide for new practice

1. **Fact.** The passage states that diet varies with where raccoons live; point to the “Eating Almost Anything” section.
2. Change it to: **The passage says scientists think dipping may soften the paws and help raccoons feel food.** The cause is presented as a scientific idea, not a settled fact.
3. The graphic can show body features; a fact such as what raccoons eat or when they use dens must come from the text.
4. **“Many Different Dens.”** Its section contains the winter details, so the heading points readers to the right part.
5. **Mostly active at night and resting during the day.**
6. The passage says not to get too close and notes that raccoons can spread disease, but that does not establish that every raccoon is dangerous in every situation. A safe answer follows the warning without adding a broader claim.
7. **Answers vary.** A fact must match the den section. An inference must be marked as a conclusion, such as several dens may give an animal more than one hiding place; it should not be called a sentence from the passage.
8. Use two source details, such as eating pet food/garbage near people and overturning trash cans or pulling down bird feeders. Cite the relevant paragraphs.
9. **Answers vary.** Credit a sentence that covers the whole passage and two accurate, located details; a single-topic sentence about one body feature is too narrow.
10. Examples include overturned trash cans, dug-up gardens, pulled-down bird feeders, or unwanted dens in homes. Each detail needs a source clue.
11. A dated wildlife survey or government research report comparing raccoon counts over time. The passage itself says numbers “may” be growing and does not give a full data table.
12. **Answers vary.** A strong response names the main idea and combines two major topics such as body/food, night activity/dens, or life near people. It paraphrases rather than copying.

**Response check:** for constructed responses, give credit for a clear answer, two accurate details from the passage, and an explanation connecting the details to the answer. NYSED explains that these responses use text evidence and are expected to be short and complete; use the linked scoring guide when assigning official-style points.

English.title: ELA week: how characters face problems — *Big Moon Tortilla* and “The North Wind and the Sun”
English.subject: English
English.contentMarkdown:
**Status:** This five-day study uses two actual texts in the 2025 NYSED Grade 3 ELA released booklet. It is a state-assessment supplement, not evidence that P.S. 230 assigned these passages. Read the complete texts and official questions in the [released booklet](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/ela/2025/2025-released-items-ela-g3.pdf); use the [official scoring materials](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/ela/2025/2025-scoring-materials-ela-g3.pdf) for released-response examples. This guide paraphrases the readings and adds new practice; it does not copy the stories.

**The readings:** Joy Cowley's story excerpt *Big Moon Tortilla* follows Marta after a chain of accidents ruins her homework and breaks her glasses. Her grandmother comforts her, repairs the glasses temporarily, and tells her several ways to think about a problem. Marta chooses to be like an eagle, which Grandmother describes as seeing a problem from farther away; Grandmother then tells her to return to her homework. The story ends with Marta's decision, not a report that she finished the work. Mary Ann Hoberman's poem “The North Wind and the Sun” gives two weather forces speaking voices. They compete to make a traveler remove his coat: the North Wind's strong gusts make him hold it tighter, while the Sun's warmth makes him take it off. These are different kinds of texts, but both show a character facing a challenge and how a choice affects what happens next.

#### Read it in simple English

In *Big Moon Tortilla*, one mistake leads to more trouble: Marta hurries toward the cookhouse, knocks over a table, loses her homework outside, and breaks her glasses while trying to save a page. Her grandmother does not solve every part at once. She helps with the glasses and tells a story about choosing how to face a problem. Marta decides to use the eagle's wide view. Keep the event chain tied to the story; do not say the homework or glasses are fixed if the passage only shows a temporary repair or Marta's next choice.

In “The North Wind and the Sun,” the two speakers make claims about their power and agree to a contest. The wind uses a forceful gust, but the traveler responds by shivering and holding his coat close. The Sun shines warmth; the traveler becomes hot and removes the coat. The poem's events show that the strongest-sounding claim does not always lead to the result a character wants.

The official released questions examine character traits and evidence in the poem, the Sun's view of its own power, and how the Wind and Sun are alike. The booklet also has questions about why parts of Marta's story matter, word meaning, her feelings, her grandmother's belief, and a summary detail. These are real NYSED examples. The new questions below are practice questions written for this guide.

#### Five-session study plan

Plan for **45–60 minutes each day**. Read from the official booklet; write printed paragraph or line numbers beside evidence. The existing [Grade 3 evidence organizer](images/grade-03/ela/g03-ela-nonfiction-evidence-organizer.png) can be reused by labeling its main-idea space “idea about facing a problem” and naming which story each evidence detail comes from.

| Day | Work | End check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Follow Marta's problem chain (45–55 min) | Read *Big Moon Tortilla* once (15 min). On a second read, mark what Marta does before the table tips, what happens to her homework, and what happens to the glasses (15 min). Put the events in order (10 min). Answer Questions 1–4 (5–15 min). | Each event comes from the story and is placed in the right order. |

Explain why Marta chooses the eagle (10 min). Try released Questions 26–31 in the booklet and check with its key (10–20 min). | The answer explains what Marta chooses and how the story shows that choice. |

Make a cause/effect chain for the coat contest (15 min). Answer Questions 11–14 (10–20 min). | The learner uses the poem's events to describe a character, not just a personal opinion. |

Separate a detail directly stated in the text from an inference about a character (10 min). Try released Questions 32–34 from the booklet; compare responses with the official scoring examples (15 min). Write a short paragraph comparing a character's choice and result in each (20 min). Answer Questions 19–20, revise, and point to the source details (10–20 min). | The paragraph states an idea, uses both readings, and explains how actions lead to outcomes. |

#### New practice questions — not copied NYSED questions

Use the booklet for text details. For each answer about a character, point to an event, line, or paragraph that supports it.

1. What was Marta rushing to do before the first accident?
2. Put these events in story order: dogs tear the papers; Marta's table tips; her glasses break; she runs to Grandmother.
3. What two troubles does Marta describe when she reaches Grandmother?
4. What temporary help does Grandmother give for the broken glasses?
5. Name two of Grandmother's examples for choosing how to face a problem.
6. What does Marta decide to do after hearing Grandmother's story?
7. Which story event best supports the idea that Marta has changed how she sees her troubles?
8. What does the phrase “spread them over the village” mean in the story's context? Use what the wind does to the papers.
9. Why does Marta start crying? Use the two problems from the passage, not only one.
10. Which detail belongs in a short summary: Marta's stomach growls, the dogs tear the papers and her glasses break, or the tortilla browns? Explain why you chose it.
11. In the poem, what does the North Wind claim about its power at the start?
12. Compare the Wind's opening claim about itself with what happens when it tries to remove the coat. What does this difference show?
13. After the Wind fails, what does the Sun do? Explain how the result connects to the Sun's earlier claim about warmth.
14. What details show that both speakers care about proving their claims? Give one detail about the Wind and one about the Sun.
15. What happens to the traveler's coat when the Wind uses force? Explain cause and effect.
16. What action does the Sun take, and how does the traveler respond?
17. What do the Wind's and Sun's different results help a reader notice about their approaches?
18. In the poem, the weather forces speak like people. Name one thing a speaker says or does that supports this.
19. Mark each as a story detail or an inference: (a) Marta chooses to be like an eagle; (b) seeing a problem from farther away may help her feel calmer; (c) the Wind's gust makes the traveler hold his coat tighter; (d) the Wind is overconfident.
20. Write a 3–5 sentence comparison: What does Marta do when she has a problem, what do the Wind and Sun do in their contest, and what does each result show?

8. The wind scatters the papers around the village. “Spread” means scattered around here.
9. Her homework has been ruined and her glasses have been broken. A complete answer names both.
10. The chain of ruined homework and broken glasses belongs in the summary because it explains the main problem. The growling stomach and browning tortilla are smaller details.
11. The Wind says it is cold and strong and claims no one can beat it. Use its opening lines.
12. The Wind says it is strong and cannot be beaten, but its gust makes the traveler pull the coat tighter. The gap between its claim and result shows that it is overconfident about what force will do.
13. The Sun comes out and warms the traveler; he becomes hot and removes the coat. This supports the Sun's earlier claim that warmth can have power.

15. The Wind's gust makes the traveler shiver and pull the coat closer, so the Wind's action has the opposite effect from the one it wants.
16. The Sun warms the traveler. He becomes hot and eventually removes his coat.

19. (a) Direct story detail; (b) inference supported by Grandmother's eagle story and Marta's choice; (c) direct poem detail; (d) inference about the Wind supported by its boast and challenge.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: How geography shapes communities
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
![World locator map with verified base boundaries and marked case-study countries China, Egypt, Nigeria, and Peru](images/grade-03/social-studies/g03-social-world-community-locator.png)

The image credits a public-domain Natural Earth base and places locator dots for four case-study countries. Use the linked source and the map key; the dots show locations, not the full size of each community. A locator map helps answer “where?” It cannot tell what every person in a country believes, speaks, eats, or does.

**Verified NYC course:** Grade 3 Passport begins with **Introduction to World Geography and World Communities**, then introduces case studies of **China, Egypt, Nigeria, and Peru**. The NYC course page says students compare communities across time and place and study geography, culture, and global citizenship. Its culture topics include social organization, customs and traditions, language, arts and literature, religion, government, and economic systems. It also names prejudice, discrimination, human rights, and social action. This is the published course scope, not confirmation of Nahid's current Passport lesson. The page links the Unit 1 guide/workbook and four case-study guides/workbooks; its digital slides require NYCPS credentials. [NYC Grade 3 Passport page and guides](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/3rd-grade).

#### Learn the ideas

**Location and place.** Location tells where something is. A map can show a country’s position, nearby countries, oceans, or major physical features. Place is the set of features that make an area recognizable; some features are physical, such as a river or mountain, and some are built by people, such as a road or bridge. Check the map title, date, legend, direction marker, and source before using it. A map’s scale or projection may change how size and distance look.

**Culture and evidence.** In the NYC course, culture includes several parts of community life—not only food, clothing, or celebrations. A source might describe a specific group, place, period, or example. Keep that boundary in your notes. Write “this source describes…” and name its subject; do not turn one example into a claim about everyone in a country. If the guide does not answer a question, record “not stated in this source” and look for another reliable source only when the teacher approves.

**Comparing communities.** A useful comparison names the same feature for each case. For example, compare the way two cited sources describe a physical feature, a form of government, or a tradition. Say whether the sources show a similarity or difference, then cite the page or image that supports the statement. Do not compare a fact from one source with a guess about another place.

**Human rights and action.** The NYC scope names prejudice, discrimination, human rights, and social action. Discuss these through the assigned guide and teacher-selected examples. Separate what the source states from your opinion. When proposing an action, name the problem supported by evidence, a helpful step, and who could take that step. Do not repeat a hurtful stereotype as if it were a fact.

#### Public-source China example: the Great Wall

The NYC China case-study guide names the Great Wall as one representative lesson topic, along with the Grand Canal, modern environmental challenges, folklore, and the Silk Road. The complete teacher guide and student workbook require NYCPS access, so this short reading uses a separate public source. It does not claim that Nahid's class is studying the Great Wall this week. [NYC Grade 3 China case-study guide description](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-3-unit-2/).

**Read in simple English:** UNESCO says that around 220 BCE, during the rule of Qin Shi Huang, people joined sections of older fortifications to make a connected defense against invasions from the north. Building work continued for many centuries, including during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). The source describes the Great Wall as a very large military structure. This account shows that the wall was built and changed over time; it was not made in one short project. UNESCO is a later summary, not a firsthand account from a builder. [UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “The Great Wall”](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/438/).

**Read the map and images:** UNESCO's maps page names Badaling, Shanhaiguan, and Jiayuguan as mapped sections. The page does not say those three names are every part of the wall. Use the map title, section labels, and date. Then inspect one photo in UNESCO's gallery and record details you can point to. The map can help locate a section; a photo can show visible features of the place. Neither one alone tells the full history or what every person thought. [UNESCO map page](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/438/maps/) · [UNESCO photo gallery](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/438/gallery/).

**Key words:** a **fortification** is a wall or other structure built to protect a place; **defense** means protection from attack; an **invasion** is an attack in which an outside army enters a place; a **dynasty** is a line of rulers from the same family or group over time; **around 220 BCE** means close to that date, not on an exact known day.

#### Five study sessions

| Session | 45–60 minute plan |
|---|---|
| 1 — Read the map | Use a teacher-approved, labeled atlas or the actual Passport map. Locate China, Egypt, Nigeria, and Peru. Read the title, legend, direction marker, and source. Add continent/ocean labels only where the map supports them. Write one location fact and one question the map cannot answer. |
| 2 — Learn the community and geography vocabulary | Read the actual Unit 1 guide/workbook when available. Use the Great Wall public-source reading above to practice fortification, defense, invasion, and dynasty. Make a two-column chart: what the NYC guide says it studies and what UNESCO says about the wall. |
| 3 — Gather case-study evidence | Read the teacher-assigned case-study pages for China, Egypt, Nigeria, or Peru. For China, use the Great Wall as the public-source practice case if the workbook is unavailable. Record the exact source, topic, and a short paraphrased fact. Complete Great Wall Questions 13–18 and check each answer against the page or map. |
| 4 — Compare fairly | Use evidence from two assigned case studies. Choose one shared category and write one similarity or difference. Check that both sides come from sources and refer to a named place, group, or time. Then discuss one course concept—human rights, prejudice, discrimination, or social action—using the actual assigned example. Complete Great Wall Questions 19–20 as a source-type and image check. |
| 5 — Teach back and reflect | Give a short talk or write a paragraph with one map fact, two case-study details, and one supported comparison. Cite page numbers or map labels. Complete Great Wall Questions 21–22, then finish with one unanswered question and one respectful way to investigate it. |

#### Supplemental source-study practice — new questions about the actual assigned course pages

These are study prompts, not copied Passport workbook questions. Complete them with the NYCPS guide/workbook or another teacher-approved source. Without that source, do not fill in missing country facts.

1. Which four case-study countries are named on the NYC Grade 3 course page?
2. What is the title/topic of Passport Unit 1?
3. Name two things a map legend can explain. Use the map’s own key.
4. Find one physical feature and one human-built feature in an assigned source. Write the page or map label for each.
5. Record one sourced fact about a community in China. Which page supports it?
6. Record one sourced fact about a community in Egypt. Which page supports it?
7. Record one sourced fact about a community in Nigeria. Which page supports it?
8. Record one sourced fact about a community in Peru. Which page supports it?
9. Choose two case studies. Compare the same category in both. What evidence supports the comparison?
10. Find an example connected to a course culture topic: social organization, custom/tradition, language, arts/literature, religion, government, or economic system. State exactly what the source covers.
11. Find the assigned example for prejudice, discrimination, human rights, or social action. What does the source say, and what does it leave unanswered?
12. Write one question the map or reading cannot answer. Name a source that might answer it, and explain why it is a better source than a guess.

#### Great Wall practice — new questions using the public source

These are supplemental questions, not copied Passport or NYSED questions.

13. What does “around 220 BCE” tell you about the date? Is it exact?
14. What did people do to earlier fortifications during Qin Shi Huang's rule, according to UNESCO?
15. What purpose does UNESCO give for joining the earlier sections?
16. What does the source say about the time span of the building work? Use one date range or period.
17. Name the three Great Wall sections listed on UNESCO's map page.
18. Does that map page say those three places are every section of the Great Wall? Explain.
19. Is UNESCO's description a firsthand account from a wall builder? Why or why not?
20. Choose one UNESCO gallery photo. Write two things you can see and one history question the photo cannot answer alone.
21. Put these source facts in time order: Ming dynasty period; sections of older defenses are joined around 220 BCE; building work continues through later centuries.
22. Fix this claim so it matches the source: “The Great Wall was built all at once and stopped every invasion.”
