Social Studies.title: Social studies week: Nigeria — adire cloth, design, and one artist
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**School-scope connection:** The public NYC Passport Grade 3 Nigeria case study names lessons on comparing Nigerian cultural and language groups, scarcity and marketplaces, and traditional adire cloth and designs, including the work of artist Nike Davies-Okundaye. This week develops the adire topic using a museum record and the artist’s foundation biography. It is a source-based supplement, not confirmation that P.S. 230 assigned this exact lesson or these exact readings to Nahid. [NYCPS Grade 3 course overview](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/3rd-grade); [WeTeachNYC, NYCDOE Passport Grade 3 Nigeria case study](https://www.weteachnyc.org/resources/resource/passport-social-studies-grade-3-unit-3/).

**Reading — student-friendly paraphrase of the named sources:**

Nigeria is a country in West Africa with many cultural and language groups. This week looks closely at one art tradition associated with Yoruba people in southwestern Nigeria. It does not describe every person or every art tradition in Nigeria.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art explains that **adire** is a Yoruba name for cloth made with a resist-dye process. In **adire eleko**, a maker paints designs on cotton cloth with a paste made from cassava flour before dyeing the cloth. The paste-covered marks resist the dye, so the design shows against the dyed cloth. A Met collection record for *Ibadandun Wrapper (Adire Eleko)* identifies its culture as Yoruba peoples, its country as Nigeria, its region as Abeokuta, and its material as cotton. The maker is listed only as a Yoruba artist; the record does not give that person’s name. The object is dated to the 20th century, not to one exact year. This is a real museum object, and it is **not** identified as a work by Nike Davies-Okundaye.

The NYC guide names Nike Davies-Okundaye as a contemporary artist connected to the adire lesson. Her foundation’s biography says that her great-grandmother taught her adire textile work and that she developed her own style. The biography says Nike founded the Nike Centre for Art and Culture in Osogbo in 1983. Because this is a biography from her own foundation, it is a first-party account about the artist and her center. It is useful evidence about how the foundation describes her life and work; it is not a neutral survey of all Nigerian artists or communities.

**Key words:** **cloth** is fabric; a **pattern** is a design that repeats or is arranged across a surface; **dye** is color added to a material; **resist-dyeing** uses a material that keeps dye away from selected parts; **artifact** is an object made or used by people; **first-party source** comes from a person or organization describing its own work or experience.

**Visual sources:** Use the existing [Grade 3 world-community locator](images/grade-03/social-studies/g03-social-world-community-locator.png) only to find Nigeria; its crowded labels are noted above, so verify the location in an atlas. Open the Met’s [African textiles gallery](https://www.metmuseum.org/exhibitions/listings/2008/african-textiles/photo-gallery) to examine the pictured adire cloth *Olokun*, and open the Met’s [*Ibadandun Wrapper (Adire Eleko)* record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/318969) to see the separate cotton artifact and its catalog details. The two objects are not by the same named artist, and neither is attributed to Nike Davies-Okundaye. No generated picture is needed: the museum’s real textile images are the visual references. Ask students to observe the actual cloth before reading the caption, and do not guess that a motif has a specific meaning unless the cited source explains it.

**Five sessions, about 45–60 minutes each:**

| Day | Lesson | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Locate and set limits | Find Nigeria in West Africa using an atlas and the world-community locator. Read the NYC course page and identify what it says about Nigeria, culture, and case studies. | Write three facts about the course scope and one sentence explaining why one Nigerian example cannot represent every Nigerian community. Record the map title and source. |
| 2 — Look closely at a textile | Open the Met gallery and study *Adire Cloth: Olokun*. Before reading the caption, list shapes, colors, repetitions, and spaces you can actually see. Then read the caption and compare. | Create an observation/inference/unknown chart. Add three visible details, two caption-supported facts, and one question the image cannot answer. |
| 3 — Explain the making process | Read the Met explanation of adire eleko and inspect the separate Met catalog record. Draw a four-step diagram: cotton cloth → cassava-starch design → dyeing → finished pattern. Label the process as a model based on the source. | Add one sentence explaining why the starch makes a resist pattern. List the material, region, and date wording from the museum record. |
| 4 — Compare sources about Nike | Read the foundation biography section about what her great-grandmother taught her and the opening of the Osogbo center. Compare those claims with what the Met catalog says about the unnamed maker of its artifact. | Make a two-source chart. Label the foundation biography “first-party” and the Met record “museum catalog.” Do not claim that either museum object was made by Nike. |
| 5 — Write a small exhibit label | Answer: “How can a textile show a skill passed between people, and what can a source tell us about that skill?” Use the Met record plus one accurate detail from the foundation biography. | Write a 5–7 sentence exhibit label with a title, one material/process fact, one place/time fact, one artist fact, and one sentence naming what the sources do not tell us. Cite each source beside its fact. |

**Independent practice — guide-written questions, not copied from Passport or the museum:**

1. What country and region does the NYC Passport course study in this case study?
2. Which people’s art tradition is the focus of this week’s adire example?
3. Does this week claim that every person in Nigeria makes adire? Why not?
4. What does the Met say the Yoruba word **adire** names?
5. What two materials does the Met name for the adire eleko design process?
6. In the described process, is the cassava-starch paste applied before or after the cloth is dyed?
7. What does the paste do in a resist-dye process?
8. What is the title of the Met object in the catalog record?
9. What material does that catalog record list?
10. What place and date range does the record give? Is the date an exact year?
11. Does the catalog name the individual maker? What does it say about the maker?
12. Is the Met object identified as a Nike Davies-Okundaye artwork?
13. What does Nike’s foundation biography say her great-grandmother taught her?
14. What center does the biography say Nike founded, and in which city and year?
15. Which source is first-party about Nike’s own center: the Met catalog or her foundation biography? Explain.
16. Name one fact the textile image can show and one fact it cannot prove by itself.
17. Why should a student avoid using one Yoruba cloth as a description of all Nigerian art?
18. Write a four-sentence exhibit label with one museum fact, one foundation-biography fact, and one limit on what the sources establish.

**Checked answers:** 1) Nigeria, in West Africa. 2) Yoruba adire cloth and design. 3) No; the course itself studies several cultural and language groups, and this is one specific tradition. 4) A type of resist-dyed cloth. 5) Cotton cloth and cassava-flour starch paste; the cloth is colored with dye. 6) Before dyeing. 7) It keeps dye away from the marked areas, helping create the design. 8) *Ibadandun Wrapper (Adire Eleko)*. 9) Cotton. 10) Abeokuta region, Nigeria; 20th century, which is a broad period rather than an exact year. 11) No personal name is given; the record identifies the maker as a Yoruba artist. 12) No. It does not attribute that object to her. 13) Adire textile work and related textile skills. 14) The Nike Centre for Art and Culture in Osogbo, founded in 1983, according to her foundation biography. 15) The foundation biography, because it is published by the organization describing its own founder and center. 16) Accept a visible pattern/color/shape as an observation; the image alone cannot prove who made it, what every motif means, or how the process was done. 17) Nigeria contains many communities and art traditions; one object is evidence about that object and its documented context, not every Nigerian person. 18) Check that the answer includes both correctly attributed facts and an explicit limit; accept different accurate wording.

**Source and attribution notes:** The Met’s [African textiles gallery](https://www.metmuseum.org/exhibitions/listings/2008/african-textiles/photo-gallery) explains adire eleko and displays *Adire Cloth: Olokun*. The Met’s [collection record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/318969) supplies the separate object’s title, maker description, material, place, and broad date. The [Nike Art Foundation biography](https://nikeartfoundation.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Nike-Okundaye-Bio-full.pdf) supplies the first-party account about Nike Davies-Okundaye and her center. These readings paraphrase the sources; they do not reproduce a school workbook. Respect source limits and identify each source in the student’s writing.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: Egypt — read the Rosetta Stone as a history source
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**School-scope connection:** NYC Passport Grade 3 is **Communities around the World**. Its public course page names Egypt as one case study, along with China, Nigeria, and Peru, and says students compare communities across time and place. This is a public-source Egypt supplement, not a claim that Nahid's class is assigned the Rosetta Stone or that this is the full Passport Egypt guide. [NYCPS Grade 3 course page and Egypt case-study link](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/3rd-grade).

**Reading — a plain-English retelling of the British Museum sources:**

The Rosetta Stone is a broken piece of a larger stone slab called a **stela**. The British Museum identifies the stone as granodiorite and dates its inscription to **196 BCE**. It came from near the town of el-Rashid, also called Rosetta, in Egypt. A council of priests issued the decree written on it for Ptolemy V, a young king in Egypt's Ptolemaic period. The British Museum's fuller account says the priests praised the king and listed honors given to him. This is one official message made in ancient Egypt; it is not a school exercise or a secret treasure map.

The same decree appears on the stone in three forms of writing: **hieroglyphic**, **demotic**, and **Greek**. The British Museum explains that the hieroglyphic writing suited a priestly decree, demotic was an Egyptian script used for everyday purposes, and Greek was the language of administration. These are not three unrelated stories. They are versions of one public decree, made so people who used different kinds of writing could read it. A museum record counts 14 hieroglyphic lines, 32 demotic lines, and 54 Greek lines on the surviving stone. The lines are different lengths, so a student should not assume that each one lines up word for word with a line in another section.

For a long time, scholars could no longer read hieroglyphs. The Greek section helped scholars work out the Egyptian writing. The British Museum's account credits Thomas Young with showing that some hieroglyphic signs represented sounds in the royal name Ptolemy. Jean-François Champollion later showed that hieroglyphs could record sounds in the Egyptian language. Their work helped people learn to read many other Egyptian writings too. The Rosetta Stone did not translate every ancient text by itself; it gave scholars a major clue.

The stone also has a story after it was made. The British Museum says French soldiers found it in 1799 while digging at a fort near Rosetta. After the French army lost in Egypt, the stone passed to the British under the Treaty of Alexandria in 1801. The British Museum says it has displayed the stone since 1802, except for one break. That is the museum's account of how the object reached its collection. The stone itself is primary evidence for the decree from 196 BCE; the museum's modern catalogue is a later explanation. A careful reader can use both while remembering that a museum record does not include every Egyptian person's point of view.

**Key words:** **stela** is an upright stone slab with writing or pictures; **decree** is an official public order or announcement; **hieroglyphic** is an ancient Egyptian writing system that uses signs, including picture-shaped signs; **demotic** is a later Egyptian script used for everyday purposes; **administration** means the work of running a government; **primary source** is an object or record made at the time being studied; **catalogue** is a museum's written record about an object.

**Look at the real object:**

![Rosetta Stone photographed for a 1922 British Museum book; the image shows the broken inscribed stone](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/The_Rosetta_Stone.jpg/500px-The_Rosetta_Stone.jpg)

*Photo from a 1922 British Museum book; the Commons file page marks it public domain. The object shown is a museum photograph, not an image made in 196 BCE. Use the [file page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Rosetta_Stone.jpg) for image details and the [British Museum catalogue](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/Y_EA24) for object facts.*

Use the existing [Grade 3 world-community locator](images/grade-03/social-studies/g03-social-world-community-locator.png) to locate Egypt among the course case studies. It is a broad locator, not a detailed Nile map. For close map work, use a classroom atlas: find northeastern Africa, Egypt, the Nile River, and the Nile Delta near Rashid/Rosetta. Do not estimate a route or distance from the small locator.

**Five study sessions — about 50–65 minutes each:**

| Day | Lesson | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Locate the case study | Read the NYC course description. On an atlas, locate Africa, Egypt, the Nile Delta, Rashid/Rosetta, and Memphis. Put a small date label, 196 BCE, beside the ancient object—not beside modern Egypt. | Sketch a simple locator with a compass direction, a title, and a source line. Write one sentence about why a map of present-day Egypt and an object from 196 BCE show different kinds of evidence. |
| 2 — Observe before reading | Look closely at the photograph. Write only what can be seen: shape, color, breaks, carved lines, and how the writing is arranged. Then read the British Museum catalogue's material, title, and date. | Make two columns: “I can see in the photo” and “The catalogue tells me.” Put at least three statements in each column. Do not guess the message from the picture. |
| 3 — Compare the writing sections | Revisit the three blocks of writing. Read the source explanation for hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek. Draw a simple top/middle/bottom diagram and label each block with the source's description. | Explain in your own words why one decree could be written in more than one form. Keep **script** (how words are written) separate from **language** (the words people use). |
| 4 — Follow the evidence and the object's route | Read the British Museum's account of decipherment and the object record. Add 196 BCE, 1799, 1801, and 1802 to a timeline, with one source beside every date. | Write two links in the story: the Greek writing helped scholars study hieroglyphs; and the museum records a later route from Egypt to Britain. Add one sentence naming a perspective the museum catalogue may not include. |
| 5 — Write a short museum label | Review the photo, atlas, source table, and timeline. Answer the practice questions. Then draft an exhibit label for a Grade 3 visitor. | Your 5–7 sentence label should identify the object and date, name the three forms of writing, explain why the Greek text helped scholars, give one later event from the stone's route, and tell one thing the image alone cannot prove. Cite the museum source. |

**Source organizer:**

| Evidence source | What it can help us learn | One limit |
|---|---|---|
| Stone and its inscription | A decree was written in three forms in 196 BCE. | The broken stone does not tell every detail about ancient Egyptian life. |
| British Museum catalogue | Object material, date, text sections, and the museum's recorded history of the object. | It is a modern museum record and presents the museum's account. |
| Atlas and locator map | Where Egypt is in Africa and where the Nile Delta lies. | A small locator cannot show exact distance or the whole ancient landscape. |
| Photograph | Visible shape, damage, and carved writing. | A photo cannot translate the inscription or prove who wrote it. |

**Practice — guide-written questions, not copied from Passport or the museum:**

1. What is the title of the NYC Grade 3 social studies course?
2. Name the four places/countries listed as Grade 3 case studies on the NYC course page.
3. Is the Rosetta Stone identified as a specific lesson in the public course overview, or is this guide using it as a public-source Egypt example?
4. What does the word **stela** mean?
5. What year does the British Museum give for the inscription?
6. What kind of stone does the British Museum catalogue name?
7. From which Egyptian town area did the museum record say the stone came? Give either name used in the record.
8. Who issued the decree written on the stone?
9. What was the decree about, in a few simple words?
10. Name the three forms of writing the British Museum describes.
11. Which form suited a priestly decree?
12. Which Egyptian script did the museum say was used for everyday purposes?
13. Which language did the museum say was used in administration?
14. Why did the Greek part help scholars study hieroglyphs?
15. What did Thomas Young show about some hieroglyphic signs?
16. What did Jean-François Champollion help scholars understand about hieroglyphs?
17. According to the British Museum, when did French soldiers find the stone?
18. What dates does the museum give for the stone passing to the British and being displayed at the British Museum?
19. Give one fact a photograph can support and one question it cannot answer by itself.
20. Write a 5–7 sentence museum label using three accurate source facts and one sentence about a source's limit or point of view.

**Checked answers and evidence guide:** 1) **Communities around the World.** 2) China, Egypt, Nigeria, and Peru. 3) It is a public-source Egypt example; the public overview names Egypt as a case study but does not name the Rosetta Stone as a required lesson. 4) An upright stone slab with writing or pictures. 5) 196 BCE. 6) Granodiorite. 7) el-Rashid/Rashid or Rosetta, near Fort Saint Julien, Egypt. Accept one named in the British Museum record. 8) A council of priests. 9) It was a decree about the king Ptolemy V and honors for him. 10) Hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek. 11) Hieroglyphic. 12) Demotic. 13) Greek. 14) Scholars could read Greek and compare it with the Egyptian writing on the same decree; the Greek text provided a key for decipherment. 15) Some hieroglyphic signs represented sounds in the royal name Ptolemy. 16) Hieroglyphs could record sounds in the Egyptian language. 17) 1799. 18) The museum says the stone passed to the British in 1801 under the Treaty of Alexandria and has been displayed in the British Museum since 1802, with one break. 19) Accept a visible feature such as the stone's broken shape or carved lines; it cannot by itself translate the writing or prove who made it. 20) Check the label for at least three accurately attributed facts plus one limit or perspective note; accept clear, original wording.

**Source and perspective notes:** The NYC course scope comes from the [NYCPS Grade 3 page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/3rd-grade); its linked case-study materials may require NYCPS access. The [British Museum object record](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/Y_EA24) supplies the date, material, place, writing sections, and collection history. Its [hieroglyphs timeline](https://www.britishmuseum.org/exhibitions/hieroglyphs-unlocking-ancient-egypt/egyptian-hieroglyphs-decipherment-timeline) and [large-print exhibition guide](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/2022-10/Hieroglyphs_unlocking_ancient_Egypt_large_print_guide_The_British_Museum_2.pdf) explain the decree and decipherment. The [Rosetta Stone photograph](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Rosetta_Stone.jpg) is from a 1922 British Museum book and is marked public domain on its file page. These student readings paraphrase those sources; no long museum or textbook passage is copied. The British Museum's catalogue documents its own account of the object's route; this unit does not treat that catalogue as every Egyptian perspective or as the full story of present-day cultural heritage debates.

Social Studies.title: Social studies week: Peru — how the Inca built with a mountain landscape
Social Studies.subject: Social Studies
Social Studies.contentMarkdown:
**School-scope connection:** NYC Passport Grade 3 names Peru as one of its **Communities around the World** case studies. This public-source companion focuses on Machu Picchu, an Inca site in Peru's Andes. The public course overview does not say Machu Picchu is the assigned Passport lesson, and the complete Peru teacher guide/workbook is not readable without NYCPS access. Use this as a documented Peru case study, not as a claim about the exact work Nafis's school assigned. [NYCPS Grade 3 course page and Peru case-study link](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/3rd-grade).

**Reading — plain-English account based on UNESCO and Peru's official tourism source:**

Peru is a country in western South America. The Andes Mountains run through the country. Machu Picchu is high in the Peruvian Andes, on the eastern side of the mountains toward the Amazon Basin. UNESCO places the site about 2,430 meters above sea level, in a tropical mountain forest. A map helps us locate the place, but it does not explain how people used it.

Machu Picchu was built in the fifteenth century, during the time of the Inca Empire. UNESCO describes about 200 structures on a steep ridge. The site has upper and lower areas, a large square, and stone terraces. Peru's official tourism site describes an agricultural area with terraces used for growing crops and an urban area with buildings. These sources show that the site joined human-made spaces with a steep mountain environment. They do not mean the whole Inca Empire lived in this one place.

Terraces are level platforms built into a slope. At Machu Picchu, rows of stone terraces follow the mountain. A student looking at a photograph can observe their shape and position. A source can tell us that terraces were used for farming. A photograph alone cannot tell us which crops grew there, who worked a certain terrace, or exactly how every terrace was used. The UNESCO record also names irrigation canals and a road-and-trail system in the wider sanctuary. When evidence does not answer a question, we should leave it open instead of making up an answer.

UNESCO says Machu Picchu was abandoned after the Inca Empire was conquered by Spain in the sixteenth century. It also says the archaeological complex was made known to the outside world in 1911. That wording is careful: it does not say that no local people knew the place existed before then. Peru's official tourism page connects the site to the Inca Empire and its continuing place in Peru. Ancient Inca history is part of Peru's past; people in Peru today live in many communities and should not be described as if all of them live as people did in the fifteenth century.

Machu Picchu is not only old buildings. UNESCO describes the protected sanctuary as both cultural and natural heritage. The larger property includes mountain slopes, peaks, valleys, forests, and animal and plant life. Its exact purpose in Inca life is still not fully known. Researchers can describe evidence—such as stone buildings, terraces, canals, and the setting—and test ideas against that evidence. A careful explanation separates what a source states from what a student infers.

**Key words:** **Andes** are a long mountain range in South America; **Inca** refers to the people and empire associated with this historical site; **terrace** is a level step or platform built into a slope; **agricultural** means connected to growing crops; **urban** means connected to a town or city; **sanctuary** is a protected area; **archaeological** means connected to learning about the past through objects, buildings, and places; **inference** is a conclusion drawn from evidence and reasoning.

**Visual study:**

![Stone terraces step across the steep green mountain landscape at Machu Picchu](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Terraces_at_Machu_Picchu.jpg/960px-Terraces_at_Machu_Picchu.jpg)

*Photo by Gedankenstuecke, “Terraces at Machu Picchu,” licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. [Photo and license details](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Terraces_at_Machu_Picchu.jpg). This is a present-day photograph; it is not an image from Inca times.*

First, list three visible observations without explaining them. Then read the [UNESCO site description and map](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/274) and compare what the written sources add. The [UNESCO property map](https://whc.unesco.org/en/documents/126939) shows the larger protected area, not a detailed plan of every building. Use the existing [Grade 3 world-community locator](images/grade-03/social-studies/g03-social-world-community-locator.png) only to find Peru on the world map; it is not detailed enough to locate Machu Picchu. A new AI-generated picture is not needed for this lesson because a reusable, attributed photograph and actual UNESCO map are available.

**Five study sessions — about 50–65 minutes each:**

| Day | Lesson | Work to save |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Find Peru and Machu Picchu | Locate South America, Peru, the Andes, and the Amazon Basin on an atlas. Open the UNESCO description and identify the stated elevation. Add Cusco only if your atlas or the Peru Travel source labels it. | Draw a simple locator with a title, north arrow, and source. Label Peru, the Andes, Machu Picchu, and the Amazon Basin using a map; put “about 2,430 m above sea level” beside the site. Don't estimate distance from the small world locator. |
| 2 — Observe the terraces | Study the photograph. Record lines, steps, walls, slope, plants, and any other visible detail. Then compare those observations with UNESCO and Peru Travel. | Make an “I see / source says / I infer” chart. Put a source beside every statement in the “source says” column. Move an unsupported guess out of the fact column. |
| 3 — Match design to place | Read the descriptions of agricultural terraces, urban areas, canals, the steep ridge, and mountain setting. Draw a simple labeled side view of a slope with terraces. It is a student diagram, not a measured plan of Machu Picchu. | Explain how a level platform changes the shape of a steep slope. State what the sources say the terraces were used for and name one detail the sources do not give about a particular crop or worker. |
| 4 — Build a careful timeline | Put “built in the 15th century,” “Inca Empire conquered by Spain in the 16th century,” and “made known to the outside world in 1911” on a timeline. Cite UNESCO beside each. Read its note that some parts of the site's role remain unresolved. | Write one supported sentence and one open question about the site. Explain why “made known to the outside world” is more careful than saying “nobody knew it was there.” |
| 5 — Make an evidence-based visitor card | Re-read the public NYC course scope, UNESCO page, Peru Travel page, map, and photo caption. Complete the practice below. | Write a 6–8 sentence visitor card: locate the site, identify its Inca history and approximate time, describe two source-supported features, explain the terraces, include one natural setting fact, and label one question as unresolved. Add source titles and a note that present-day Peru is not the same as fifteenth-century Inca society. |

**Evidence organizer:**

| Claim | Evidence to use | Check before writing |
|---|---|---|
| Machu Picchu is high in the Andes. | UNESCO site description and an atlas/map. | Do not mix meters with feet or claim an exact height from a photo. |
| Terraces are part of the site. | Photo, UNESCO, and Peru Travel. | The photo shows their shape; a written source supports their agricultural use. |
| People built and used the site. | UNESCO's account of Inca construction, buildings, terraces, canals, and paths. | Do not claim every structure's exact purpose; some questions remain unsettled. |
| Machu Picchu is part of both cultural and natural heritage. | UNESCO site description. | Name one human-made feature and one natural feature as evidence. |

**Practice — guide-written questions, not copied from Passport or a school workbook:**

1. What title does NYC give to the Grade 3 social studies course?
2. Which four world case studies does the public NYC course page name?
3. Is Machu Picchu named as a required lesson in that public overview, or is it this guide's public-source Peru example?
4. On which continent is Peru?
5. What mountain range includes the site?
6. About how high above sea level does UNESCO say Machu Picchu is?
7. Which direction from the Andes does the UNESCO description connect with the upper Amazon Basin?
8. In which century does UNESCO say Machu Picchu was built?
9. Which empire is the site linked to?
10. What two broad areas does Peru's official tourism site use to describe the citadel?
11. What does UNESCO say the stone terraces cross or follow?
12. What does Peru Travel say the agricultural terraces were used for?
13. Name one feature, besides terraces, that UNESCO lists in the wider sanctuary.
14. What happened to the Inca Empire in the sixteenth century, according to UNESCO?
15. What careful phrase does UNESCO use about the site's 1911 history?
16. Why should a student avoid writing, “Nobody knew Machu Picchu existed before 1911”?
17. Name one natural feature of the protected sanctuary and one human-made feature.
18. What is one question about Machu Picchu that UNESCO says remains unresolved?
19. What can the photograph show directly, and what needs a written source?
20. Write a 6–8 sentence visitor card using at least three supported facts, one visual observation, and one source limit or uncertainty.

**Checked answers and evidence guide:** 1) **Communities around the World.** 2) China, Egypt, Nigeria, and Peru. 3) It is this guide's public-source example; the public overview names Peru as a case study but does not specify Machu Picchu as a required lesson. 4) South America. 5) The Andes. 6) About 2,430 meters above sea level. 7) On the eastern slopes/side of the Andes. 8) The fifteenth century. 9) The Inca Empire/civilization. 10) Agricultural and urban areas. 11) A steep ridge/mountain slope. 12) Growing/cultivating crops. 13) Accept a road or trail system, irrigation canals, a large square, buildings, or mountain/forest habitat, if correctly attributed to UNESCO. 14) UNESCO says the empire was conquered by the Spanish in the sixteenth century. 15) The archaeological complex was “made known to the outside world” in 1911. 16) That sentence claims too much and erases the possibility of local knowledge; UNESCO's wording only describes when it became known outside the region/world. 17) Accept mountain forest, peaks, valleys, or the Andes as natural; terraces, stone buildings, canals, or roads as human-made. 18) Accept the exact role it played, or its role in astronomy or domestication of wild plants; UNESCO says these remain unresolved. 19) The photo can show visible terraces, stonework, vegetation, or mountain shape; written sources are needed for the date, Inca history, function, and what a feature was used for. 20) Check for 6–8 sentences, three accurate sourced facts, an observation grounded in the image, and one clearly named limit/uncertainty. Accept different wording.

**Source and perspective notes:** The [NYCPS Grade 3 course page](https://sites.google.com/schools.nyc.gov/social-studies-and-civics/resources-by-grade/elementary/3rd-grade) names Peru as a course case study; it does not publicly identify Machu Picchu as a specific lesson. [UNESCO's Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu page](https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/274) supplies location, elevation, dates, terraces, structures, natural setting, and unresolved questions. Its [property map](https://whc.unesco.org/en/documents/126939) shows the protected-area boundary. The [Peru Travel Machupicchu page](https://www.peru.travel/attractions/machu-picchu) describes agricultural and urban sectors and the terraces' crop use; it is Peru's official tourism source. The photograph is by **Gedankenstuecke** and licensed **CC BY-SA 4.0**; credit the photographer and link the [license/source page](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Terraces_at_Machu_Picchu.jpg), and mark any edits. These readings paraphrase public sources rather than copy a Passport workbook. Do not describe contemporary Peru as a single culture or treat the Inca past as the whole story of the country.

Science.title: Science week: Water on Earth and the water cycle
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
![Unlabeled water-cycle model with clouds, land, plants, and water, with arrows for students to trace](images/grade-03/science/g03-science-water-cycle.png)

Use as a tracing task, not a labeled answer key. Add evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, and collection only after checking each arrow against NASA's explanation below; the PNG itself has no process labels.

**Verified P.S. 230 topic:** the October 2025 Grade 3 newsletter says both teachers studied **Water on Earth**. It lists weather, clouds, atmosphere, cloud formation, and the water cycle; one report also names temperature and air pressure. The newsletter is an archived last-year example, not a current unit calendar. NASA explains that water continually moves among land, oceans, and air through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation, with plants also releasing water vapor. [October 2025 P.S. 230 newsletter](https://app.smore.com/n/qjeu0); [NASA water-cycle explanation and diagram](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/the-water-cycle/).

#### Learn the ideas

Water exists as ice (solid), liquid water, and water vapor (gas). The water cycle is the ongoing movement of water among Earth's surface, underground, and the air. The Sun supplies energy that helps drive this movement. Water changes form and place; it is not newly made each time a cloud or puddle appears.

- **Evaporation:** liquid water changes into water vapor and moves into the air. The vapor is a gas and usually cannot be seen.
- **Condensation:** water vapor cools and changes into tiny liquid droplets. Droplets can gather into a cloud. Water on the outside of a cold cup can also form when water vapor in nearby air cools on the cup.
- **Precipitation:** water falls from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. Which form falls depends on conditions in the air.
- **Runoff and soaking in:** water that reaches land can flow over the ground toward streams and rivers, or soak into soil and become groundwater. Some remains in lakes and other surface water.
- **Transpiration:** plants take in water and release some water vapor from their leaves. NASA identifies this as another route by which water enters the air.

The cycle does not move every drop through one neat circle. A drop may evaporate, freeze, move underground, or be taken up by a plant. NASA gives Lake Superior to Massachusetts as one possible path: water can rise into the air and later fall as rain far away. That is an example of a possible route, not a record tracking one particular drop. A model should show branching paths and explain what it leaves out.

#### Five study sessions

| Day | 45–60 minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Read and trace | Read the NASA water-cycle article with an adult and inspect its diagram. Make a three-column word chart: process, what happens to water, and evidence from the source. Trace one possible route from water at the surface to the air and back. |
| 2 — Observe evaporation | Put equal measured amounts of water in two identical, clear, labeled containers. Leave one in a sunny place and one in a shaded place in the same room; keep both safe from spills. Mark levels at the start and after a set time. Record temperature/location differences if known. The result can vary; do not write an expected result as an observation. |
| 3 — Observe condensation | An adult places ice and water in a clean, dry cup. Watch the outside and record where droplets appear. Draw the cup and surrounding air. Explain which water changed form and where the droplets came from, using the NASA definition of condensation. |
| 4 — Model many paths | Use the unlabeled model and NASA's diagram. Add arrows and labels for evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, soaking into the ground/groundwater, and transpiration. Make at least two different routes. Use arrows to show movement, and add a small note for something the diagram does not show. |
| 5 — Explain from evidence | Write a short explanation of how water can move from Earth's surface into the air and back. Include at least four process words, two facts from NASA, one actual observation from the investigation, and one limit of the model. Explain how the Lake Superior/Massachusetts route is possible without claiming NASA tracked one drop. |

#### Supplemental practice — new questions based on NASA's explanation

Use the NASA source, your model, and your recorded observations. These are new practice questions, not copied school or state-test items.

1. A puddle's liquid water changes into water vapor. What process is this?
2. Water vapor cools and forms tiny liquid droplets. What process is this?
3. Name two forms precipitation can take.
4. Give two different places water can go after precipitation reaches land.
5. What is one way plants move water into the air?
6. What supplies much of the energy that drives the water cycle?
7. Is water vapor the same as visible cloud droplets? Explain the difference in state.
8. On a cold cup, droplets form on the outside. What is a source-based explanation for the droplets?
9. Your model shows a cloud, rain falling, and a river. Add one route by which some rainwater could move underground.
10. NASA describes a possible route from Lake Superior to rain in Massachusetts. Does this prove that NASA followed one named water molecule? Why?
11. In the container investigation, the shaded container loses less water than the sunny one. Write one observation and one possible explanation. What else should be measured before claiming the Sun caused the difference?
12. Name one thing the cup or drawing model cannot show about the whole water cycle.

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer guide

1. **Evaporation:** liquid water changes into water vapor.
2. **Condensation:** water vapor cools into liquid droplets.
3. **Any two supported forms:** rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
4. **Any two:** flow over land as runoff, soak into soil/groundwater, collect in a lake/river, or return to the air by evaporation. The source allows different routes.
5. **Transpiration:** plants take in water and release water vapor from leaves.
6. **The Sun.** It supplies energy that drives much of the cycle.
7. **No.** Water vapor is gas and usually invisible; cloud droplets are tiny liquid drops.
8. **Water vapor in the surrounding air cooled at the cold cup and condensed into liquid droplets on its outside.**
9. Draw an arrow from land surface into soil and label “soaking in” or “groundwater.” Do not draw it entering the cup/cup model.
10. **No.** NASA gives a possible path to show how water can travel; it does not claim it tracked one named molecule.
11. **Observation:** the marked level changed by the recorded amount in each container. **Possible explanation:** the sunnier place may have warmed the water more and supported faster evaporation. Before claiming cause, record temperature and keep container, start amount, exposure time, and other conditions as similar as possible. If those conditions were not controlled, report the limit.
12. **Answers vary:** examples include the full atmosphere, exact temperatures and wind, underground pathways, the long time scale, or all possible routes. The learner must explain the model's limit.

**Visual:** use NASA's actual water-cycle diagram alongside the unlabeled practice model. Check every arrow and label against NASA. The student-created diagram is a learning model, not a NASA diagram and not a complete picture of all water pathways.

Science.title: Science week: interacting forces, magnets, and simple machines
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
![Unlabeled diagrams show a lever and carts with equal or unequal opposing force arrows](images/grade-03/science/g03-science-force-and-lever.png)

Use the left panel to label fulcrum, effort, and load. Use the cart panels to compare balanced and unbalanced forces; labels are not baked into this image, so verify them with the lesson text.

**Verified P.S. 230 classroom example:** the May 2026 newsletter says one Grade 3 class began **Interacting Forces**, including simple and complex machines. It is a dated report from one teacher, not proof of Nahid’s current unit or exact class experiments. New York State Grade 3 standards also cover balanced and unbalanced forces and magnetic interactions. [P.S. 230 May 2026 newsletter](https://app.smore.com/n/b3muj) · [New York State P–12 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf).

#### Learn the ideas

A **force** is a push or a pull. A force can change an object's motion: it can start or stop it, make it speed up or slow down, or change its direction. A moving object can keep moving in the same way when the forces on it are balanced; “balanced” does not mean that no forces act. For example, a resting book has gravity pulling down and the desk pushing up. If the forces on an object are unbalanced, its motion changes. In a drawing, arrows can show the direction of pushes or pulls, but do not label them equal unless the evidence supports that claim.

Magnets can push or pull some objects without touching them. The effect depends on the objects and the poles facing each other. Like poles push apart; unlike poles pull together. A magnet does not attract every object or every metal. Test one object at a time and record the actual result rather than deciding from color or appearance.

A **simple machine** is a tool that can change how a force is applied. In a lever, the support point is the **fulcrum**; the force you apply is the **effort**, and the object being moved is the **load**. A ramp is another simple machine. A machine can make a task easier in one way, but it does not remove the need for a force. The exact class model and labels should follow the assigned P.S. 230 lesson.

#### Five study sessions

| Day | 45–60 minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Observe motion | Read the assigned science text or teacher-approved NYS standard summary. On a clear, flat surface, gently push a toy car once. Mark its starting place and direction. Make a before/after drawing and list what you observed; do not add a distance unless you measured it. |
| 2 — Model balanced forces | Draw an object at rest with arrows for the forces acting on it. If using a safe classroom demonstration, compare the object's motion before and after gentle opposing pushes. Do not treat hand strength as a measuring tool: describe the setup and observed motion rather than claiming exact equality. |
| 3 — Test magnetic interactions | With an adult and a classroom-approved magnet, make a prediction for each safe object, test one at a time, and record whether it moved toward the magnet. Then bring magnet ends together slowly and record whether they pull together or push apart. Keep magnets away from electronics, medical devices, and small children. |

Science.title: Science week: life cycles and traits — investigate the class organism
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Verified P.S. 230 classroom example:** the May 2026 newsletter says one Grade 3 class completed a **Life Cycle Investigation**. It does not name the organism, book, or experiment, so this guide does not guess those details. The New York State Grade 3 expectation is to model that organisms have different life cycles but share the broad pattern of birth, growth, reproduction, and death. Use the organism and source assigned by the teacher. [P.S. 230 May 2026 newsletter](https://app.smore.com/n/b3muj) · [New York State P–12 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf).

**Important limit:** the P.S. 230 newsletter does not identify the class organism. The monarch butterfly below is a real, source-verified example for practice; it is **not** claimed to be the school's organism or assigned text. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes the monarch's four stages as egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), and adult. Eggs are laid on milkweed; caterpillars feed on milkweed. [USFWS monarch life cycle](https://www.fws.gov/species/monarch-danaus-plexippus).

![U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service photograph of monarch eggs and caterpillar development stages on milkweed](https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/styles/max_1300x1300/public/images/2016-08/20676.jpg?itok=7eRGKWbm)

Photo: Brett Billings/USFWS, public domain. The image helps identify egg and caterpillar stages; use the written source to learn the complete four-stage cycle. [USFWS image details and usage rights](https://www.fws.gov/media/stages-monarch-caterpillar-development-0).

![Blank four-stage life-cycle frame with arrows; students add the class organism and stages from their assigned source](images/grade-03/science/g03-science-life-cycle-organizer.png)

#### Learn the ideas

A **life cycle** is the set of stages an organism passes through as it grows and reproduces. Different organisms can have different stages. A monarch changes form as it develops: egg → larva (caterpillar) → pupa (chrysalis) → adult butterfly. This is complete metamorphosis. The adult can lay eggs, so the cycle can begin again. A circular arrow in a model means the pattern repeats; it does not mean each individual butterfly lives forever.

The USFWS source says monarch eggs are laid on milkweed and hatch after about 2–5 days. The caterpillar feeds on milkweed and grows through five stages before it forms a green-and-gold chrysalis. It emerges as an adult after about 6–14 days in the chrysalis. A second USFWS source gives a broader 9–18 day range for the caterpillar stage and says temperature affects the total time. These are ranges, not a promise that every monarch takes the same number of days. Adult monarchs need nectar from flowers. Do not handle wild caterpillars for this lesson; use the source image/video and teacher-approved classroom materials.

A **trait** is a feature of a living thing, such as a body part or color pattern. Some traits are passed from parents to offspring; experiences and surroundings can also affect organisms. A picture of a monarch's colors shows what it looks like, but the picture alone does not prove why it has those colors. To say a trait is inherited or affected by the environment, use a source or investigation that supports the statement. If the class organism's source does not explain a trait's cause, write “not determined by this source.”

#### Five study sessions

| Day | 45–60 minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Read and record | Read the teacher-assigned source for the actual class organism. Record its name, source title, page, and stages. If the source is unavailable, use the monarch source above as a clearly marked practice example. |
| 2 — Build the cycle | Arrange the monarch stages in order and draw arrows. Add a short source fact beside each stage. Use a loop only to show that an adult can lay eggs and the pattern can repeat. Make a separate model for the class organism only if its source gives the stages. |
| 3 — Use time and evidence | Make a timeline from the source ranges: egg about 2–5 days, caterpillar about 9–18 days, chrysalis about 6–14 days. Label these as approximate ranges. Explain why they do not give an exact duration for every butterfly. |
| 4 — Study traits carefully | Identify two visible features in the USFWS photo or assigned class image. Describe only what can be seen. Find a source fact about each feature. If the source does not explain its cause, write “not determined”; do not infer inheritance from appearance alone. |
| 5 — Explain and compare | Explain the monarch's four stages using at least three cited details. Compare one feature of its life cycle with the class organism only if a second source is available. Add one limit of a drawing/photo and one question the source leaves open. |

#### Supplemental practice — new questions based on USFWS sources

These are not copied P.S. 230 questions. Use the cited USFWS pages and image; answer about the monarch practice example unless the teacher assigns the actual class organism.

1. Put the monarch's four stages in order.
2. Which plant do monarchs lay eggs on, according to USFWS?
3. What does the monarch caterpillar eat, according to USFWS?
4. What stage comes after the caterpillar and before the adult?
5. About how long does a monarch egg take to hatch in the USFWS species description?
6. What does the USFWS source say about the time a monarch spends in a chrysalis?
7. Why should time ranges in a life-cycle chart be labeled “about” or “approximately”?
8. Is “the pictured insect is an adult monarch” supported if the photo shows eggs and caterpillars? Explain.
9. What happens after an adult monarch lays eggs?
10. Does the newsletter identify which organism P.S. 230 students investigated? What should a student do if asked to name it?
11. Does the photo alone prove how a visible feature was inherited or caused? What evidence would help?
12. Name one thing the photo or cycle drawing leaves out about a living monarch.

Science.title: Science week: weather patterns and climate
Science.subject: Science
Science.contentMarkdown:
**Grade-level scope:** This week supports New York Grade 3 expectations 3-ESS2-1 and 3-ESS2-2. Students use a table or bar graph to describe typical weather in a season, then combine information to describe and compare climates in different regions. The standard names temperature, precipitation, and wind direction as possible data; it limits student graphs here to pictographs and bar graphs. This is grade-level support, not evidence that P.S. 230 is teaching this exact unit now. [New York State Grades 3–5 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/3-5-science-learning-standards.pdf).

**Archived school example:** P.S. 230's October 2025 newsletter says Grade 3 classes studied Water on Earth, including weather, clouds, the atmosphere, cloud formation, and the water cycle. This is a dated report from last school year. It does not establish Nahid's current lesson, assigned book, or class sequence. [P.S. 230 October 2025 newsletter](https://app.smore.com/n/qjeu0).

#### Learn the ideas

**Weather is what the air and sky are like at a certain time and place.** It can include temperature, clouds, rain or snow, wind, and humidity. A forecast is an estimate of what the weather may be soon. A weather observation is what a person or instrument measures or sees at a stated time and place. “It is raining at 3 p.m. in Brooklyn” is a weather statement. It needs a date and place to be useful evidence.

**Climate is the pattern of weather over many years.** It includes the usual range of conditions and how those conditions change from season to season. Scientists use long records to describe a place. The National Weather Service tables below use 1991–2020 climate normals, a 30-year period. A normal describes a long-term pattern; it is not today's weather and does not promise what tomorrow or next summer will be like. One snowy day does not prove that a place has a cold climate, just as one warm day does not prove that its climate is warm.

**Look for patterns, not one matching day.** A table can show a typical temperature or amount of rain for each month or season. A bar graph can make the pattern easier to see. Before comparing bars, read the title, labels, units, and scale. Temperature is measured in degrees; precipitation is measured as a depth of water, such as inches. Keep those units separate. The National Weather Service's Central Park chart uses different scales for temperature and precipitation, so bar heights from the two scales cannot be compared directly.

**Climate can differ from place to place.** Here are two official station summaries for the same 1991–2020 period. These are measurements summarized for the Central Park and Phoenix weather stations; they do not describe every neighborhood or every day in either city.

| Weather station | 1991–2020 average annual temperature | 1991–2020 average annual precipitation |
|---|---:|---:|
| Central Park, New York | 55.8°F | 49.52 inches |
| Phoenix, Arizona | 75.6°F | 7.22 inches of rain |

Sources: National Weather Service [Central Park normals](https://www.weather.gov/media/okx/Climate/CentralPark/nycnormals.pdf) and [Phoenix normals](https://www.weather.gov/psr/19912020Normals). The NWS Central Park table reports annual precipitation; the Phoenix table calls its measure annual rainfall. The values are both depths in inches, but the labels above preserve the source wording.

The Central Park normals also list seasonal average temperatures: winter 36.2°F, spring 53.2°F, summer 75.2°F, and autumn 58.4°F. From this table, summer is the warmest season on average and winter the coolest. The difference is `75.2 − 36.2 = 39.0°F`. That is a difference between seasonal averages, not the hottest and coldest temperatures ever measured.

![National Weather Service chart of Central Park monthly temperature and precipitation normals](https://www.weather.gov/images/okx/Climate/CentralPark_TempPrecip_Normals.png)

*Read the temperature and precipitation scales separately. Students can make their own four-bar graph of the seasonal average temperatures from the table above. Source chart: National Weather Service, Central Park 1991–2020 normals.*

#### Five study sessions

| Day | 45–60 minute lesson and work |
|---|---|
| 1 — Sort observations and patterns | Read “Learn the ideas.” Sort these statements into **weather**, **climate**, or **not enough information**: “It rained at school this morning”; “Central Park's 1991–2020 winter average was 36.2°F”; “It will rain tomorrow.” Explain why the last statement is a forecast, not a climate fact. Record the evidence words: date, place, time period, and unit. |
| 2 — Graph seasonal temperatures | Copy the four Central Park seasonal averages into a table. Draw a bar graph with a title, season labels, °F, and an even scale that starts at 0. Use a ruler. Add one sentence saying which season is warmest on average and one comparing it with winter. Check each bar against the table. |
| 3 — Read a real weather observation | Open the National Weather Service observation page for Central Park or, with an adult, record local conditions from a weather instrument. Write the date, local time, place/station, temperature and unit, sky condition, wind direction if reported, and precipitation if reported. Mark anything the source does not report as “not given”; do not guess. This is one day's weather. Compare it with the seasonal normal only after matching the measurement and unit. [NWS Central Park observations](https://www.weather.gov/wrh/timeseries?site=KNYC). |
| 4 — Compare two climates | Use the Central Park and Phoenix table. Underline the warmer annual average temperature; circle the larger annual precipitation amount. Write two complete evidence sentences with station names, numbers, and units. Then explain one limit: these station summaries do not tell the weather on a particular day or describe every spot in either city. |
| 5 — Make a claim and check it | Write a short claim about one way the two station climates differ. Support it with both rows in the table. Add a reason the evidence supports the claim and one question the table cannot answer. Revise any sentence that treats a 30-year average as a forecast or treats one day's weather as a climate pattern. |

#### Supplemental practice — use the tables and sources above

These questions were written for this guide. They are not P.S. 230 assignments or copied test questions. Use the cited NWS data; for questions about a current observation, use the date and station you recorded on Day 3.

1. In your own words, what is weather?
2. What is climate, and what years are the Central Park normals based on?
3. Is “It snowed in Brooklyn on one Tuesday” enough evidence to describe Brooklyn's climate? Why or why not?
4. Which Central Park season has the highest average temperature in the table? Which has the lowest?
5. How many degrees Fahrenheit higher is the summer average than the winter average?
6. Which station has the higher annual average temperature? Give both values and the unit.
7. How many degrees Fahrenheit apart are the two annual average temperatures?
8. Which station summary lists more annual precipitation? How many inches more?
9. If one Central Park day is warmer than 36.2°F, does that mean the winter normal is wrong? Explain.
10. What two measurements or sky details did you record on Day 3? Include date, time, place, and units where needed. *(Answers depend on the real observation.)*
11. Your observation page reports temperature and wind but no rain amount. What should you write for precipitation?
12. Why must you read the temperature and precipitation scales separately on the NWS chart?
13. What does the seasonal bar graph help a reader see? Name one thing it cannot show.
14. Is the Central Park table a forecast for next winter? What does it describe instead?
15. Write one claim comparing the two stations. Include one temperature value and one precipitation value as evidence.
16. A classmate says, “Phoenix had one rainy day, so its climate is wetter than Central Park's.” What is wrong with this reasoning? Use the table.
17. Name one extra source or kind of data you would need to compare seasonal rainfall in both places.
18. A weather report says wind is coming from the west. What does “west” tell you, and what information would help you draw its direction on a map?

Science.answerKeyMarkdown:
#### Checked answer key

1. **Weather** is the condition of the air and sky at a certain time and place, such as temperature, clouds, rain, or wind.
2. **Climate** is a place's pattern or usual range of weather over many years. The Central Park normals use **1991–2020**.
3. **No.** It describes one event on one day. Climate is a long-term pattern; many years of data are needed.
4. **Summer, 75.2°F; winter, 36.2°F.**
5. `75.2 − 36.2 = 39.0`; **39.0°F**.
6. **Phoenix:** 75.6°F. **Central Park:** 55.8°F. Phoenix has the higher annual average.
7. `75.6 − 55.8 = 19.8`; the station averages are **19.8°F apart**.
8. **Central Park.** `49.52 − 7.22 = 42.30`; the listed totals differ by **42.30 inches**. The source labels the Central Park value precipitation and the Phoenix value rainfall.
9. **No.** A normal is a long-term average, not a temperature every day. Individual days can be warmer or colder.
10. **Answers vary.** Check that the student reports the actual observation with its date, time, place/station, and units, and does not invent details missing from the source.
11. Write **“not reported”** or **“not given.”** Do not change missing data into zero or guess.
12. They use **different quantities and units**. One scale is temperature; the other is precipitation. The bar heights cannot be compared directly across the scales.
13. It helps show how the **seasonal average temperatures compare**. It cannot show every day's temperature, the exact weather on a date, or the hottest temperature ever recorded.
14. **No.** It summarizes long-term conditions from 1991–2020; it does not say what next winter's weather will be.
15. **Answers vary.** A complete response should name both stations and accurately use at least one temperature and one precipitation value with units. Example: “Phoenix's annual average temperature is higher (75.6°F compared with Central Park's 55.8°F), while Central Park's listed annual precipitation is greater (49.52 inches compared with Phoenix's 7.22 inches of rain).”
16. **One rainy day is short-term weather, not a climate record.** The 1991–2020 station summaries list 49.52 inches for Central Park and 7.22 inches of rain for Phoenix.
17. **Monthly or seasonal precipitation normals for both stations** (or another source that gives the same measure, time period, and units for each place).
18. **West tells the direction the wind comes from.** A map with a direction marker or compass rose would help draw the direction correctly.

**Visual and source note:** Use the official NWS Central Park chart above, plus the student-made four-bar seasonal graph. The graph uses real NWS seasonal averages; students draw it themselves, so no generated picture is needed for this topic. NASA's [water-cycle overview](https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/the-water-cycle/) can support a review connection between precipitation and Earth's water cycle. For the difference between weather and climate, see the NWS elementary [Climate Really Can Be Elementary](https://www.weather.gov/media/owlie/2018_Elementary.pdf) lesson. Climate change is outside the assessment boundary for 3-ESS2-1, so this week does not turn into a climate-change lesson.

Science.passage: Water moves among Earth’s surface, the air, living things, and the ground. Sunlight can warm liquid water so some changes into water vapor and rises; this is evaporation. Water vapor cools and forms tiny droplets in clouds; this is condensation. Water can return to the surface as rain or snow; this is precipitation. It may flow over land as runoff or soak into the ground. Plants also release water vapor. The cycle has many paths, so it is better understood as a system than as one simple circle.

[NYSED 2025 Grade 3 Math released questions (PDF)](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf), PDF p. 9 (printed test p. 4).


## Five-session study units

Each unit is designed for about **45 minutes a day for five days**. Use the NYSED booklet as the actual reading/question source. Any extra drills below are labeled new practice; they are not school worksheets or NYSED questions. The archived P.S. 230 newsletter topics are from 2025–26 and may not be this year's sequence.

## Mathematics

### P.S. 230 program evidence

P.S. 230 says it uses **TERC Investigations in Number, Data, and Space** as the basis of its math program, with real-world problem solving. This confirms a program, but not a current Grade 3 unit or lesson. [P.S. 230 mathematics](http://www.ps230.org/mathematics); [TERC curriculum overview](https://investigations.terc.edu/the-curriculum/).

### New York State Grade 3 scope (not a school book map)

- **Multiplication and division:** represent equal groups/arrays; use known facts and properties; solve word problems with products and quotients within 100.
- **Place value and operations:** work with three-digit numbers and use place-value strategies for addition and subtraction.
- **Fractions:** understand unit fractions and fractions as equal parts of a whole or set; compare simple fractions using models.
- **Measurement and data:** time, mass, liquid volume, measurement conversions within the grade’s system, scaled graphs, and area/perimeter.
- **Geometry:** classify shapes using attributes and understand that area can be measured with square units.

For actual released state question examples, open the [NYSED Grade 3–8 released math tests](https://www.nysed.gov/state-assessment/past-grades-3-8-tests) and select Grade 3. The question booklet and answer/item maps are NYSED’s real questions; this file does not invent replacement questions.

### Two exact released questions with answer reasoning

- **Elapsed time / measurement:** NYSED Question 37 asks about Cassandra waking at 6:15 and a bus arriving half an hour later. Add 30 minutes: the bus arrives at **6:45 a.m.** This is an explanation of the published prompt, not a new question. [2025 Grade 3 math booklet, Question 37, printed page 10](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf).
- **Equal groups / division:** Question 38 gives 6 bags with 6 cookies in each bag, then asks how many bags are needed for the same number of brownies if each brownie bag holds 4. First find 6 × 6 = 36; then 36 ÷ 4 = **9 bags**. [2025 Grade 3 math booklet, Question 38, printed page 11](https://www.nysedregents.org/ei/math/2025/2025-released-items-math-g3.pdf).

## Science

### New York State Grade 3 performance expectations

- **Forces and interactions:** observe how balanced/unbalanced forces and magnetic interactions affect motion.
- **Inheritance and variation:** compare traits in organisms and consider which traits are inherited, learned, or influenced by the environment.
- **Life in environments:** use evidence about organisms and habitats to explain survival and ecosystem relationships.
- **Weather and climate:** use weather data and patterns to describe climate and compare regions.

These are the Grade 3 standards’ science topics, not proof that P.S. 230 uses Amplify or follows a particular order. The state provides the standards and Grade 5/8 released science tests, but not a Grade 3 state test. [NYS P–12 Science Learning Standards](https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/curriculum-instruction/p-12-science-learning-standards.pdf); [NYSED science standards/resources](https://www.nysed.gov/standards-instruction/science).
